The post Hackers Use ARTEX AI to Breach WorkOS and Access Customer Slack Conversations appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
WorkOS has confirmed unauthorized access to an internal sales application, exposing customer contact information and records of business conversations. The company detected the incident on October 30, 2026, and published a security bulletin on November 2. Its investigation identified an AI-assisted offensive security framework used to automate reconnaissance and exploitation attempts.

Founder and CEO Michael Grinich said the attack involved ARTEX, an AI-powered framework that automates offensive security tasks. His statement on X adds detail to the company’s security bulletin, which describes an AI-assisted framework that automates reconnaissance and exploitation attempts without naming the tool.

The affected application provided access to names, email addresses, phone numbers, job titles, and company affiliations stored in customer relationship management systems. It also contained customer account histories and sales relationship information.

Customer communications included summaries and excerpts from sales calls, support discussions, and customer Slack conversations. Operational metadata covered customers’ use of WorkOS products, including product usage and connection or directory health.

WorkOS Confirms Data Breach

These categories describe information available through the application, not a confirmed record-by-record account of everything accessed.

WorkOS is reviewing affected records to determine the impact on individual organizations. The statement supplied with the disclosure says there is no evidence that WorkOS application data or production services were accessed or impacted. The investigation currently points to CRM and customer support information.

The incident comes amid growing abuse of automated security-testing tools. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant describe ARTEX as a multi-agent platform that turns broad attacker goals into commands. Its agents can test permissions, map networks, adjust failed commands, and continue through several attack stages with limited human input.

Earlier Cyber Security News coverage of ARTEX agents explains how attackers have used the framework for Active Directory discovery, credential attacks, and lateral movement. These are observations from separate investigations, not confirmed steps in the WorkOS breach.

Wiz research also documented agents downloading application files, discovering internal API routes, and testing authentication controls. Related coverage of ARTEX targeting Microsoft 365 shows how stolen application credentials can support attacks across customer environments. Neither report establishes attribution for WorkOS.

WorkOS disabled external access to the affected application, began reviewing access controls across internal tools, and retained an independent digital forensics and incident response firm. It will contact affected customers directly as findings are verified.

Exposed conversation details could make phishing messages more convincing. WorkOS advises customers to verify unexpected requests before sharing sensitive information or taking action, even when messages reference real colleagues or support discussions.

The post Google Dismantles 1.3 Million Device XCPE Botnet, Bans Android TV Maker Over Preinstalled Malware appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Google and industry partners have dismantled the XCPE botnet, which enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes through preinstalled malware. In a November 2 report, Google linked the operation with high confidence to Videostrong Technology, accusing the Android device maker of deliberately building and running the backdoor for profit.

According to Google’s technical investigation, Videostrong sold access to criminal affiliates that installed advertising fraud tools, proxy software, and further malware.

Google banned the company, including future subsidiaries and affiliates, from producing certified Android devices or supplying software to certified vendors.

1.3 Million Device XCPE Botnet Dismantled

The backdoor, named x.cpe or com.oemservice, was built into device firmware and ran with Android system privileges. Removing its installed package did not clear the infection because it could reinstall from the /oem/ partition after a reboot. Google said hidden code loaded after first boot helped bypass security checks.

Its three-stage design separated remote control from malware execution. The backdoor passed instructions to com.abc.nexus, a loader that configured affiliate modules.

Those modules turned devices into proxy exit points, generated fake advertising views, or installed more backdoors. This separation also helped keep malicious activity harder to detect.

Control traffic used MQTT, a lightweight messaging protocol. Google identified mqtt.szbboys[.]com on ports 3885–3887. Operators could silently install apps, execute shell commands, capture screens, and inspect networks.

Researchers also observed stolen account details and system logs, injected keystrokes, and commands that opened remote shell access. The malware could disable Google Play Protect verification.

Disruption Reaches Beyond XCPE

Google worked with Japan’s National Police Agency, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Plume, Synthient, and TrendAI. Legal action targeted XCPE servers and control domains serving more than a dozen affiliate malware families.

Google estimates these wider takedowns will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, separate from XCPE’s 1.3 million boxes.

The findings follow earlier Google legal action against BadBox 2.0, which affected over 10 million uncertified Android devices. Earlier BADBOX infections involving 190,000 Android devices also exposed the risks of compromised connected hardware. These earlier counts should not be combined with XCPE’s total.

Most XCPE infections involved Android TV boxes, but researchers also found affected telehealth equipment, karaoke machines, and digital signs. Google has changed its device review process and is improving firmware integrity checks following the discovery.

The takedown disrupts control infrastructure, rather than proving every device is clean. Google urges buyers to choose reputable manufacturers, consult its certified partner list, use trusted app stores, and keep Play Protect enabled. It also warns against apps offering payment for sharing unused bandwidth.

Brazilian cryptocurrency exchange Mercado Bitcoin suspended deposits and withdrawals on November 2, 2026, after detecting a security incident in one of its systems. Blockchain security firm Hypernative flagged more than $40 million in suspicious transfers across at least 10 blockchains, raising questions about the scope of the breach. The post Mercado Bitcoin Suffers Cyberattack as Researchers Flag $40 Million in Suspicious Crypto Transfers appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Brazilian cryptocurrency exchange Mercado Bitcoin suspended deposits and withdrawals on November 2, 2026, after detecting a security incident in one of its systems.

Blockchain security firm Hypernative flagged more than $40 million in suspicious transfers across at least 10 blockchains, raising questions about the scope of the breach. The exchange has not confirmed that amount as its actual loss.

In its official statement, Mercado Bitcoin said it quickly contained the incident early Monday morning. The company said customers suffered no harm and no data leaked. It described the service suspension as a protective measure while its teams investigate, trace assets, and work with authorities.

According to reports, Opsek founder Pablo Sabbatella shared findings describing transfers from wallets linked to Mercado Bitcoin into fresh addresses. The affected networks included Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, Tron, Polygon, Arbitrum, Avalanche, BNB Chain and Stellar. Researchers said the activity covered at least 10 chains in total.

Mercado Bitcoin Suffers Cyberattack

Most of the reported outflows occurred between 06:19 and 06:53 UTC, a 34-minute window. Earlier Bitcoin activity reportedly began around 02:15 UTC, when funds from deposit addresses started moving to addresses linked to the suspected attacker.

The preliminary count included approximately 2,852 ETH, 106 BTC, 10,700 SOL and 6.7 million XLM, alongside more than 200 other tokens. These figures remain researcher estimates rather than amounts verified publicly by Mercado Bitcoin.

Researchers described the movements as ordinary transfers rather than a smart contract exploit. That distinction puts attention on how the transactions received valid signatures. However, the available findings do not establish how the attacker obtained signing access or which internal system was compromised.

The incident follows other exchange wallet breaches covered by Cybersecurity News, including the Bitget hot wallet hack. That case involved unauthorized transfers affecting hot and warm wallet infrastructure. It offers industry context, but does not establish a shared attack method or attacker in the Mercado Bitcoin incident.

Mercado Bitcoin later published destination addresses covering Ethereum-compatible networks, Bitcoin, Solana, Stellar and Tron. The exchange said it released them to help identify and track funds on public blockchains. Such tracking also featured in the Bitfinex hack investigation, which documented how investigators followed stolen cryptocurrency through laundering activity.

As Bitcoin Magazine reported, Mercado Bitcoin had not announced a reopening time or disclosed the affected system. The unresolved issue remains the gap between suspicious wallet movements and confirmed losses. Its statement that customers were unharmed should not be read as confirmation that no exchange assets were taken.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Miami, United States, November 2nd, 2026, CyberNewswire

Prisma Browser for Business joins Guardz to connect browser protection with email, identity and endpoint security, helping security teams investigate and respond to threats across the workspace

Guardz, the Agentic Workspace Security platform built for managed service providers (MSPs), today announced the integration of Prisma Browser for Business from Palo Alto Networks.

The integration connects browser protection with email, identity, endpoint, data and user risk, helping small businesses prevent threats and giving security experts the platform to streamline autonomous unified detection, investigation, and response to incidents across the workspace.

Employees rely on browsers to access business applications, handle company information and use AI tools.

But attacks often cross these environments: a phishing email can direct an employee to a fake login page, exposing credentials and putting connected accounts at risk. 

With Prisma Browser for Business built into Guardz, MSPs and the Guardz 24/7 managed detection and response (MDR) team can investigate related activity as a unified incident.

If an employee clicks a phishing link, Prisma Browser for Business can block the malicious page, while Guardz correlates the browser event with the original email, related Microsoft 365 activity, and endpoint telemetry to support investigation and response for a single identity.

“Identity is the new center of gravity in cybersecurity, and the browser has become the primary gateway to the modern workspace. Traditional security tools operate in silos, leaving critical gaps in visibility and response,” said Dor Eisner, CEO and Co-Founder of Guardz.

“Together with Palo Alto Networks, we’re advancing a new era of identity-centric security operations, connecting signals across identity, browser, email, endpoint, and data into a unified security fabric that is powered by agents. Guardz enables MSPs to autonomously investigate, correlate, and respond to threats across the entire workspace, while giving small businesses the freedom to embrace AI securely and thrive. This is the future of cybersecurity: identity-centric, unified data fabric, and built for autonomous defense at scale,” Eisner added.

Browser Protection Across the Workspace

Powered by Prisma Browser for Business, the integration brings Palo Alto Networks’ browser security technology into the wider security service MSPs manage through Guardz. Capabilities include:

  • Phishing and session-theft protection: Inline machine-learning phishing detection and Advanced URL Filtering help block malicious pages, including fake login pages and attacks designed to steal live session tokens.
  • Malware and extension security: WildFire file analysis helps detect malicious files, while browser security scans uploads and downloads and identifies risky extensions.
  • Connected investigation and response: Browser events are linked with email, identity and endpoint signals to support incident investigations through Guardz’s 24/7 MDR service.
  • Simplified deployment: Guardz streamlines provisioning, setup and default configuration so MSPs can deploy browser protection within minutes.

The streamlined deployment has also impressed early-access MSPs. “The rollout through our RMM was super smooth.

Within minutes, the Prisma Browser for Business extension was on every Chrome and Edge profile, and it was quick and easy to configure and deploy,” said Kevin Kehoe of Datawise Networks.

“For most small businesses, the browser is now the office. Working with Guardz brings Prisma Browser for Business into the security these organizations receive from the providers they already trust.

It connects our browser protection with the wider coverage and support their MSP delivers, helping safeguard the applications and information employees use every day,” said Shivam Srivastava, VP Product at Palo Alto Networks.

AI Usage and Control

As employees increasingly use browser-based generative AI tools, small businesses need practical ways to manage which services are permitted and how company information is shared.

Guardz AI Usage and Control capabilities let technicians apply client-specific policies, including restrictions on copying, pasting, uploading and downloading files by website or category.

Complementing these controls, Guardz has introduced an AI usage report that gives MSPs a per-client view of AI tool usage based on all signals. The controls help enforce usage policies, while the report provides visibility into adoption.

About Guardz

Guardz delivers Agentic Workspace Security, helping MSPs protect the small businesses they serve.

The platform unifies protection across identities, email, endpoints and browsers, alongside adaptive security awareness and user risk, connecting signals around each identity to give security teams the context to act.

The Guardz 24/7 agentic MDR provides triage and response at machine speed, supported by an elite research and threat hunting team. Learn more at guardz.com.

About Palo Alto Networks

Palo Alto Networks is the world’s cybersecurity leader. We innovate to outpace cyberthreats, so organizations can embrace technology with confidence.

We provide next-gen cybersecurity to thousands of customers globally, across all sectors. Our best-in-class cybersecurity platforms and services are backed by industry-leading threat intelligence and strengthened by state-of-the-art automation.

Whether delivering Next-Generation Firewalls, pioneering Agentic AI security, or driving continuous frontier defense via Unit 42, we are committed to helping safely navigate the evolving digital landscape.

Omri Hurwitz

omri@omrihurwitz.com

articles.title: Hackers Could Exploit iPhone BootROM Flaws to Compromise Cryptocurrency Wallet Security
articles.description:
Older iPhones used to store cryptocurrency seed phrases could expose owners to physical attacks that airplane mode cannot stop. OneKey founder Yishi has warned that wiping an aging iPhone and keeping it offline does not make it a secure cold wallet. The concern involves BootROM flaws that let attackers run code before iOS starts. However, […]

The post Hackers Could Exploit iPhone BootROM Flaws to Compromise Cryptocurrency Wallet Security appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Older iPhones used to store cryptocurrency seed phrases could expose owners to physical attacks that airplane mode cannot stop. OneKey founder Yishi has warned that wiping an aging iPhone and keeping it offline does not make it a secure cold wallet.

The concern involves BootROM flaws that let attackers run code before iOS starts. However, this access does not automatically reveal protected wallet secrets. A seed phrase is the recovery secret that controls access to a cryptocurrency wallet.

Yishi’s warning focuses on people keeping that secret on older Apple hardware, often believing that removing network access removes the main security risks. These attacks instead depend on someone gaining physical access to the device.

The checkm8 exploit affects older iPhones through the iPhone X. A newer exploit, usbliter8, extends BootROM attacks to Apple’s A12 and A13 chips, including the iPhone XS, XR, iPhone 11 family, and second-generation iPhone SE. Researchers disclosed usbliter8 in June 2026.

BootROM is the first code a device runs when switched on. It is built into the chip during manufacturing, so Apple cannot replace the vulnerable code through a normal iOS update.

Cybersecurity News previously covered the usbliter8 BootROM vulnerability, explaining how it breaks the application processor’s trusted boot process.

An attacker places a compatible iPhone into Device Firmware Update mode and connects special USB hardware. Carefully crafted USB traffic causes memory corruption, allowing attacker-controlled code to run before the operating system loads. Public demonstrations have used a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 board, showing that the required hardware need not be expensive.

iPhone BootROM Flaws

The technical weakness combines faulty USB controller behavior with missing memory restrictions during early startup. On affected chips, USB writes can reach memory outside their intended area.

Researchers then redirect execution and load unsigned boot software, bypassing checks that normally restrict devices to Apple-approved code.

The important limit is that usbliter8 does not directly compromise Apple’s Secure Enclave, the separate security component protecting sensitive keys and passcode operations. Researchers say encrypted user data remains behind additional barriers even after the main processor’s boot chain is compromised.

Wallet theft would therefore require further weaknesses, access to decrypted information, or another attack against remaining protections.

Yishi warned that weak passwords and outdated software can increase exposure. His warning describes a possible attack path, not evidence that every affected iPhone wallet can be emptied through BootROM access alone.

Physical USB risks also extend beyond BootROM exploits. Earlier ChoiceJacking research showed how malicious charging equipment could manipulate input and approve data connections on vulnerable devices. That is a separate attack, but it reinforces why an offline phone still needs careful handling.

Owners should check their device model, install available security updates, and avoid treating airplane mode as a complete defense. Updates cannot rewrite vulnerable BootROM, but they still address weaknesses elsewhere in the software. Strong device passcodes and wallet passwords remain important additional barriers.

Anyone concerned that a stored seed was exposed should generate a new seed in a trusted environment and transfer funds. Creating another address from the original seed does not remove the underlying risk.

articles.title: Hackers Using Microsoft Teams Messages and Calls to Trick Users and Gain Remote Access to System
articles.description:
Hackers are using Microsoft Teams messages and voice calls to impersonate IT support staff, persuade employees to approve remote access, and move deeper into corporate networks. Two intrusions investigated by Microsoft show how a seemingly routine help desk conversation can lead to stolen data and access to highly privileged accounts. The attacks did not exploit […]

The post Hackers Using Microsoft Teams Messages and Calls to Trick Users and Gain Remote Access to System appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are using Microsoft Teams messages and voice calls to impersonate IT support staff, persuade employees to approve remote access, and move deeper into corporate networks.

Two intrusions investigated by Microsoft show how a seemingly routine help desk conversation can lead to stolen data and access to highly privileged accounts.

The attacks did not exploit a Microsoft Teams vulnerability. Instead, they combined social engineering, legitimate remote-support software, and weak Active Directory Certificate Services configurations.

This Windows service, commonly called AD CS, issues digital certificates that can authenticate users and computers, making insecure settings particularly valuable to attackers.

Microsoft researchers identified malicious JavaScript and Python scripts used for initial access and documented portable runtime variants supporting the intrusions.

Their October 30 investigation described two separate certificate-abuse paths after the attackers secured remote control. Microsoft has not attributed the activity to a named threat actor.

Hackers Using Microsoft Teams Messages and Calls

Both incidents started with attackers posing as help desk personnel through Teams chats and calls. Support-themed display names and organization-themed tenant names made external accounts appear familiar.

The approach mirrors earlier Teams and Quick Assist attacks that used trusted workplace tools to persuade employees to hand over control.

The attackers guided employees into approving an interactive remote-support session, primarily through Quick Assist. That approval marked the critical turning point: the intruder could operate the workstation directly.

Microsoft’s example also showed “External” and “Scam suspected” call indicators, highlighting warnings employees should examine before accepting unexpected support requests.

Once connected, the attacker placed an archive in the Downloads folder, created an update-themed staging directory under the user’s profile, and extracted the files. Portable Python, Bun, or Java runtimes then executed attacker-controlled code.

One renamed executable retained metadata identifying it as Bun, showing why a reassuring filename alone cannot establish whether software is safe.

The staged components checked Windows information, network settings, and running processes before contacting domain infrastructure.

Similar Teams help desk calls have previously supported malware delivery and internal reconnaissance, but Microsoft stressed that investigators must validate each incident’s certificate activity rather than infer it from runtime use alone.

Certificate Abuse, Data Theft, and Defensive Priorities

In the first incident, the attacker exploited an ESC1-vulnerable certificate template. Its settings allowed a low-privileged requester to supply another identity and obtain an authentication certificate for that account.

The initial phishing wave targeted three users, compromised one workstation, and produced certificates for three highly privileged accounts.

About 90 minutes after disruption, another wave targeted 16 users and compromised a second workstation. The attacker obtained certificates for eight additional privileged accounts.

Microsoft Defender blocked more than 1,000 subsequent SMB file-access attempts, but DCSync activity had already begun while containment was taking effect.

One privileged account excluded from automated containment remained usable. The attacker used it to reach a file server and run a renamed Rclone utility, copying files to an external SFTP destination.

The transfer command used 20 concurrent transfers and selected files up to three years old. The second incident followed ESC8 instead. PetitPotam forced a domain controller to authenticate to an attacker-controlled system.

The attacker relayed that NTLM authentication to AD CS Web Enrollment, obtained a domain-controller certificate, and used certificate-based Kerberos authentication to acquire a ticket-granting ticket.

Following Defender alerts, the customer isolated the workstation; no further progression was observed. Defenders should connect Teams interactions with remote-session records, process activity, certificate issuance, and Kerberos events.

Earlier reporting on Teams collaboration feature abuse also explains how collaboration logs help reconstruct these timelines. Employees should verify unexpected support requests through a known internal channel before granting access.

Microsoft recommends restricting external Teams access and unapproved remote tools, reviewing certificate-template permissions, and following its AD CS relay guidance.

Enrollment endpoints should require HTTPS and Extended Protection for Authentication. Responders must revoke unauthorized certificates and separately review Kerberos tickets: resetting passwords alone does not remove certificate-backed access.

Containment exclusions also need immediate review, because leaving one privileged identity available can preserve the attacker’s route even when other accounts are blocked.

articles.description:
Northflank urged customers to rotate all platform secrets after reports of unauthorized AI API key use, warning that environment variables across workloads, secret groups, and global settings may have been exposed. Northflank is investigating a security incident involving reported misuse of AI keys but has not confirmed the entry point, identified an attacker, or disclosed […]

The post Northflank Security Breach Leads to Unauthorized AI API Key Usage, Customers Urged to Rotate Secrets appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Northflank urged customers to rotate all platform secrets after reports of unauthorized AI API key use, warning that environment variables across workloads, secret groups, and global settings may have been exposed.

Northflank is investigating a security incident involving reported misuse of AI keys but has not confirmed the entry point, identified an attacker, or disclosed affected customers. Its credential rotation warning remains precautionary, not confirmation of widespread theft.

Northflank’s published timeline begins with a Wiz threat alert at 11:43 UTC on October 30, 2026. Engineers reviewed the alert one minute later and deployed an initial network policy patch at 12:02 UTC.

Further patches followed at 12:50 and 13:05 UTC, and the team requested support from the Wiz incident response team at 13:00 UTC.

The timeline does not explain what those patches fixed. A network policy change alone does not establish how attackers entered the platform or reached customer secrets.

Northflank Security Breach

Northflank subsequently instructed users to treat environment variables as compromised and restrict public access to add-ons where enabled. Environment variables can hold API keys, database passwords, and other application credentials.

Similar exposure concerns surfaced in the recent Railway security incident, where customers were also advised to replace stored secrets after possible unauthorized access.

Northflank said the reported activity may fit a wider pattern of attacks targeting AI credentials. It pointed to similar IP addresses in Wiz’s “Black October” report, which described incidents across nine AI developer platforms during October.

Wiz found a shared focus on stored environment variables but identified no single vulnerability connecting the attacks. The financial risk comes from LLMjacking, where attackers use stolen credentials to consume paid AI services at the victim’s expense.

Previous reporting on LLMjacking attacks shows how compromised cloud keys can support unauthorized model access and resale. However, Northflank has not published a confirmed loss total or linked its incident to a named resale operation.

Customers should revoke existing credentials through the issuing providers, generate replacements, and update affected Northflank secrets and workloads.

Northflank also asked users to review AI provider usage and billing records for unexpected activity, then report suspicious usage to its support team and the relevant provider.

Secret rotation is now available for PostgreSQL, MongoDB, MySQL, Redis, MinIO, and RabbitMQ add-ons. Northflank also enabled audit logs for all customers, including free users, giving more teams access to records that may help their investigation.

The immediate priority is replacing all potentially exposed credentials, not only AI keys already showing abuse. Northflank’s latest guidance still covers secrets across workloads, shared secret groups, and global settings while its investigation remains open.

articles.title: POC Released for Windows WinSock Ancillary Privilege Escalation Vulnerability
articles.description:
A public proof-of-concept exploit for CVE-2023-21768 shows how attackers with local access can gain SYSTEM privileges through the Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock. Researchers Valentina Palmiotti, known as chompie, and Ruben Boonen published the code. Their complete exploit targets vulnerable Windows 11 22H2 systems. The release concerns a vulnerability patched in January 2023, not […]

The post POC Released for Windows WinSock Ancillary Privilege Escalation Vulnerability appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A public proof-of-concept exploit for CVE-2023-21768 shows how attackers with local access can gain SYSTEM privileges through the Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock.

Researchers Valentina Palmiotti, known as chompie, and Ruben Boonen published the code. Their complete exploit targets vulnerable Windows 11 22H2 systems.

The release concerns a vulnerability patched in January 2023, not a newly disclosed Windows flaw. IBM published the researchers’ technical analysis on March 21, 2023.

The vulnerability carries a CVSS score of 7.8 and requires low-level local privileges, with no user interaction. It does not provide a direct route into a computer over the internet. The flaw sits in afd.sys, a Windows kernel driver that handles requests from the WinSock networking interface.

According to IBM’s technical analysis, the researchers compared driver versions from December 2022 and January 2023 to understand Microsoft’s fix. Only one function, AfdNotifyRemoveIoCompletion, appeared to have changed, helping them narrow their investigation.

The older code failed to check a memory pointer supplied from a user application. That missing check let a local attacker write to kernel memory, where Windows stores sensitive system data.

Microsoft’s updated code added validation to ensure that pointers from user mode reference suitable user-space memory rather than protected kernel addresses.

POC for Windows WinSock Ancillary Vulnerability

The researchers said they diagnosed, reproduced, and turned the flaw into a working exploit in about one day, despite having no previous experience with this driver.

Their findings show how comparing patched and unpatched software can reveal enough detail to build an attack quickly.

The public GitHub repository describes the code as a demonstration. Its complete privilege escalation chain works on vulnerable Windows 11 22H2 installations, while the underlying memory-write capability works across vulnerable systems.

These are separate claims, and the repository does not promise full exploit compatibility with every affected Windows version. To move from a limited memory write to broader control, the exploit changes Windows I/O ring objects. These objects support queued input and output work.

The technique builds on research by Yarden Shafir and enables kernel memory reads and writes. The exploit then replaces a target process’s security token with one carrying SYSTEM privileges.

IBM also reported that 360 IceSword Lab found a different exploit in the wild in January 2023. That sample used the ProcessSocketNotifications interface rather than the researchers’ direct driver approach. This report does not establish that attackers used the published GitHub code.

Administrators should verify that affected devices received Microsoft’s fix or later applicable updates. IBM’s demonstration also worked without being blocked by HVCI, showing why that protection should not replace patching.

Related coverage includes CVE-2024-38193 exploitation and the CVE-2025-32709 WinSock zero-day. Both involve the same driver, but are separate flaws with different causes and patches.

articles.description:
Synology NAS devices are facing C3RB3R ransomware attacks linked to 2024 security flaws, prompting the company to urge users to update outdated DiskStation Manager versions and packages. The warning followed reports from the 360 Security Team and Solar Emergency Response Team on October 29. Victims found their files encrypted with the .L0CK3D extension and a […]

The post Hackers Exploit Patched Synology NAS Vulnerabilities to Deploy C3RB3R Ransomware and Encrypt Files appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Synology NAS devices are facing C3RB3R ransomware attacks linked to 2024 security flaws, prompting the company to urge users to update outdated DiskStation Manager versions and packages.

The warning followed reports from the 360 Security Team and Solar Emergency Response Team on October 29. Victims found their files encrypted with the .L0CK3D extension and a ransom note named read-me3.txt.

Security teams provisionally identified the ransomware as C3RB3R. The available reporting does not establish how many devices have been compromised.

The Synology security advisory, tracked as Synology-SA-24:20, covers three vulnerabilities disclosed following Pwn2Own 2024. Published on November 5, 2024, it received several updates as fixes became available across DSM branches.

Although Appinn described the weaknesses as fixed by December 2024, Synology’s revision history shows that several patches arrived during November.

Cyber Security News previously examined the critical CVE-2024-10441 flaw in Synology DSM, which carries a CVSS score of 9.8 and allows unauthenticated remote code execution without user interaction.

Synology NAS Hit by C3RB3R Ransomware Attacks

The advisory also lists CVE-2024-50629, a webapi flaw that lets remote attackers read limited files, and CVE-2024-10445. This update certificate validation flaw lets an adjacent attacker write limited files. These carry scores of 5.3 and 4.3, respectively.

Public reporting has not established which individual vulnerability was used in each ransomware incident or whether attackers combined them.

Early coverage raised concerns because Solar reportedly investigated an affected device running DSM 7.4.1-90080 Update 1. At that stage, researchers were still examining the entry point and had not ruled out an unknown vulnerability.

The later report attributed Synology’s findings to older, patched weaknesses. The published accounts do not explain the apparent mismatch or confirm a new zero-day attack.

Synology NAS devices have faced ransomware threats before. Cyber Security News covered the Diskstation ransomware investigation, involving criminals who targeted Synology storage systems. That separate case provides background on the threat to NAS users. However, the available reports do not establish any connection to C3RB3R.

Synology’s advisory lists fixed releases including DSM 7.2.2-72806-1, 7.2.1-69057-6, 7.2-64570-4, 7.1.1-42962-7, and 6.2.4-25556-8. These are historical patch thresholds, not a recommendation to stop updating. Administrators should install the latest release supported by their NAS model and update official packages and third-party components.

Appinn’s initial incident report recommends removing direct internet access to DSM management and SSH, using a VPN for remote connections, and checking for unusual logins, unknown administrators, and scheduled tasks.

It also advises enabling two-factor authentication and keeping independent offline or off-site backups. For affected users, those separate backups may provide a route to recover encrypted files. Updating remains necessary, but it does not itself restore files already encrypted by ransomware.

articles.title: Hackers Exploit ChatGPT’s Popularity With Fake Billing Notices That Target Credit Cards and OTPs
articles.description:
Hackers are impersonating OpenAI in fake ChatGPT Plus billing emails that lead users to payment pages designed to steal credit card details and one-time passwords. The campaign combines convincing subscription warnings with a live operator who can decide when to request a verification code, potentially helping approve an unauthorized payment. The emails claim a subscription […]

The post Hackers Exploit ChatGPT’s Popularity With Fake Billing Notices That Target Credit Cards and OTPs appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are impersonating OpenAI in fake ChatGPT Plus billing emails that lead users to payment pages designed to steal credit card details and one-time passwords.

The campaign combines convincing subscription warnings with a live operator who can decide when to request a verification code, potentially helping approve an unauthorized payment.

The emails claim a subscription payment failed and urge recipients to update their billing information. This pressure mirrors other AI brand impersonation campaigns that exploit trust in popular services to collect financial information.

In this operation, the checkout page keeps victims waiting while an attacker controls what appears next. Researchers from Fortra identified the phishing operation and documented its infrastructure in research published on October 26, 2026.

Importantly, they observed phishing, not malware deployment: no executable download or compromise of victims’ computers was seen during the investigation.

Hackers Exploit ChatGPT’s Popularity With Fake Billing Notices

The attack begins with an email posing as an OpenAI payment notice. Links pass through tracking services or redirect wrappers before reaching a fake checkout hosted on short-lived WordPress instances.

Researchers found the same landing page reused across multiple recipients within a sending wave, suggesting shared infrastructure behind separately tracked messages.

The checkout imitates a payment form, recognizing card brands and formatting card numbers, expiration dates, and security codes as users type.

Similar WordPress payment phishing schemes have used convincing checkout interfaces to steal card data and verification codes, although Fortra did not establish a connection to those operations.

After submission, the page sends the card number, expiration date, security code, and cardholder name to the server. It then displays a loading animation indefinitely.

The captured code explicitly instructs the page to keep the spinner running rather than process a response or advance automatically.

Meanwhile, the browser repeatedly contacts an operator dashboard, maintaining the victim’s session and checking for instructions.

A human operator can redirect the victim to a one-time-password capture page, display an error, or end the session. One test lasting four minutes and three seconds generated 969 requests, mostly dashboard polling traffic.

This creates an opportunity to capture a bank verification code while the victim believes a subscription update is underway.

Comparable real time OTP interception appears in other payment-fraud kits, but the observed ChatGPT operation uses repeated polling to receive instructions. Capturing a code could help authorize fraud; it does not mean every submission produces a successful transaction.

Fortra found identical client-side code and a shared application identifier across independently deployed sites examined roughly a week apart.

Sites disappeared and were replaced during the investigation. Whether attackers purchased hosting accounts themselves or compromised existing customer sites remains unresolved.

The infrastructure also complicates investigation. Unexpected requests received generic errors, while a token-generating path appeared to influence access.

Researchers reported that interception-based analysis disrupted the session flow, whereas passive browser inspection captured the payment submission and polling behavior without breaking it.

For defenders, recurring page structures and dashboard traffic offer stronger detection opportunities than isolated addresses. Broader live financial phishing operations demonstrate why stolen verification codes need urgent attention.

Users should verify billing through their account rather than an email link, while organizations should investigate matching messages and report fraudulent hosting. Broad infrastructure blocks require care because legitimate customers share the platform.

articles.title: Hackers Impersonate ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity AI Bots to Hunt for Passwords and API Keys

The post Hackers Impersonate ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity AI Bots to Hunt for Passwords and API Keys appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are posing as trusted artificial intelligence bots to search websites for passwords, API keys, and cloud credentials.

The campaign uses the names of ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, and other AI services to disguise automated scanning, testing whether businesses will let requests through simply because they appear to come from a familiar provider.

The operation highlights a weakness in how organizations recognize automated visitors: a claimed identity is not proof of origin.

Similar AI crawler impersonation tactics have appeared in attacks against exposed development servers, where scanners used forged bot identities while looking for sensitive files.

Here, the disguise supports credential hunting rather than ordinary web crawling. Cequence researchers identified the malicious scanning campaign and linked it to a single actor impersonating about 32 AI bots.

In an October 28 report, CQ Prime research director Will Glazier said the actor reached 48% of Cequence-protected organizations receiving any AI bot traffic on one October day. The report describes a scanner, not a newly identified malware family.

Hackers Impersonate ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity AI Bots

Running from a major cloud provider, the scanner rotated through identities associated with OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Perplexity, and others.

Instead of reading normal pages, it requested configuration files, cloud credential files, private SSH keys, and server environment data. Researchers observed a target list containing roughly 90 file paths.

The distinction matters because these files can provide access beyond the website itself. Previous exposed environment file attacks have shown how leaked cloud credentials can support privilege escalation and data theft.

Cequence’s findings establish credential-seeking activity, however, not confirmed theft or subsequent compromise in this campaign. Each scanning address issued between 50 and 190 requests in roughly eight seconds before moving on.

The actor worked through targets individually, around the clock, and first requested random, meaningless paths to identify websites that returned responses for every request.

Activity affected financial services, retail, telecommunications, energy, and software organizations from at least late September through late October.

The impersonation became clear when researchers compared behavior across requests. One machine claimed to represent several unrelated AI providers within seconds, while the scanner cycled evenly through all 32 identities.

Fake Claude identities also reused Anthropic’s crawler contact address, even when claiming to represent a different Claude agent. Shared infrastructure and technical fingerprints connected the activity across targets.

Why Identity Verification Matters More Than IP Blocklists

Infrastructure turnover made address-based defenses difficult. The actor used more than 300 cloud addresses in one day and nearly 400 during one week.

None of the addresses observed in late September appeared again a month later. External threat feeds flagged many addresses during their use, but the scanner had usually moved elsewhere by then.

This campaign involves outsiders pretending to be agents, unlike AI agent credential exposure caused by legitimate tools handling secrets during routine work.

Both problems make identity and access controls important, but they require different investigations: defenders must distinguish forged visitors from genuine agents whose permissions or data handling create risk.

The scanner also distorted traffic measurements. At several organizations, it generated more than 80% of requests labeled as AI bot traffic.

That does not mean genuine AI services launched the attacks; it shows how trusting a visitor’s self-description can turn malicious scanning into apparently legitimate activity in security dashboards.

Cequence recommends verifying agents through signed requests, published address ranges, or direct integrations. Teams should also inspect behavior, particularly requests for credential files, and keep secrets, staging systems, and administration sites away from public access.

Broader AI agent identity controls address ownership and permissions, but a familiar bot name alone should never justify access.

articles.title: Hackers Use CyberStrikeAI Agents to Automate Windows Domain Takeovers and Credential Theft
articles.description:
Hackers are now using an AI-driven command framework called CyberStrikeAI to break into Windows networks and take over entire domains. Education organizations in Africa and Latin America were among the confirmed victims. The tool lets a language model decide which commands to run, so the operator no longer types each step by hand. CyberStrikeAI is […]

The post Hackers Use CyberStrikeAI Agents to Automate Windows Domain Takeovers and Credential Theft appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are now using an AI-driven command framework called CyberStrikeAI to break into Windows networks and take over entire domains.

Education organizations in Africa and Latin America were among the confirmed victims. The tool lets a language model decide which commands to run, so the operator no longer types each step by hand.

CyberStrikeAI is an open-source, Go-based platform built for penetration testing. Criminals have already turned it toward real targets, and earlier reports showed how attackers targeted Fortinet FortiGate devices with the same framework.

This new campaign shows the tool being used for something bigger: moving from a single weak server to full control of a network.

Analysts at Securelist identified the campaign during routine threat monitoring. They described it as one of the first public cases of a language model being used inside a live intrusion.

The human operator sets a broad goal, and the AI model on the control server picks the tools, writes the commands, and reads the results. The malware on the victim machine is a plain implant with no AI inside it.

Hackers Use CyberStrikeAI Agents

The intrusion began with a person. The operator got into a compromised SQL Server, collected basic host details, dropped tools, and scanned the network. That took almost a day, and then the attackers went quiet for about two weeks.

When they came back, the CyberStrikeAI agent took over. Within two minutes it set up persistence through a scheduled task named SystemUpdate and finished local checks. Over the next five hours it mapped the domain using PowerShell and LDAP queries.

It also collected data needed for Kerberoasting and AS-REP Roasting, two methods for cracking account passwords. Other reports show how attackers coordinate 44 AI agents with this same platform, which suggests the approach is spreading.

After a short pause of a few days, the final phase ran in under an hour. The agent moved sideways through SMB and WMI, dumped credentials from many machines, and exported database content.

It pulled passwords from registry files and from the LSASS process using the comsvcs.dll MiniDump function. After it compromised the built-in domain administrator, it ran DCSync and Golden Ticket techniques with a renamed Mimikatz tool.

The whole job, from agent install to domain admin, took only three to four days. The attackers tried to stay hidden. They encoded commands in Base64, split scripts into several files, and rebuilt them with certutil.

They also named one beacon svchosts.exe so it looked like a normal Windows process. Some scripts contained Chinese comments, and the attackers used the Chinese service dnslog.cn to find victim IP addresses.

Server restarts mostly fell within UTC+8 business hours. Together these clues suggest a Chinese-speaking operator, but Securelist could not link the activity to any known group.

Why Defenders Can Still Catch It

The methods themselves are not new. The agent used well-known tools, and the AI mainly made the work faster and easier. Because the model runs on the attacker’s server, defenders will not see AI traffic or odd resource use inside their network. They will see the same actions a human intruder would take.

That means ordinary detection rules still work. Teams should watch for remote scheduled tasks created with schtasks.exe, LSASS memory access, and WMI or WinRM commands from unusual hosts.

A DCSync attack steals password hashes by posing as a domain controller. Event ID 4662 helps catch it when the request comes from a system that is not a real domain controller. Rotating the krbtgt account twice after any domain admin compromise cancels forged Golden Tickets.

Defenders should also check for commands running from the sqlservr.exe process, since that was the likely way in. They should patch and lock down exposed SQL Servers and turn on LAPS.

They should also limit replication rights and keep logs for process launches, PowerShell activity, and logons. Microsoft recently described AI agents targeting Microsoft 365 tenants, so cloud accounts linked to the domain need the same care.

articles.title: Hackers Hijack Swedish Supermarket Fridges and Raise Freezer Temperatures to 55°C
articles.description:
Hackers have reportedly targeted refrigeration systems at Swedish supermarkets, leaving stores with spoiled food after freezers reached temperatures as high as 55°C. Several ICA locations and six Coop stores were affected overnight into November 2, forcing staff to clear damaged stock and restore cooling systems. The incidents follow similar attacks against French supermarkets in October, […]

The post Hackers Hijack Swedish Supermarket Fridges and Raise Freezer Temperatures to 55°C appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers have reportedly targeted refrigeration systems at Swedish supermarkets, leaving stores with spoiled food after freezers reached temperatures as high as 55°C.

Several ICA locations and six Coop stores were affected overnight into November 2, forcing staff to clear damaged stock and restore cooling systems. The incidents follow similar attacks against French supermarkets in October, although no connection has been confirmed.

According to Swedish broadcaster SVT, ICA Nära store manager Mats Olsson found water on the floor when he arrived at his shop in Böda, Öland. He reported a freezer temperature of 55°C, with refrigerators and freezers knocked out and their contents ruined.

Swedish Stores Face Food Losses

Affected ICA stores included locations in Sjöbo, Tomelilla, Brösarp and Sankt Olof in Skåne. Reports also covered Öland, Värmland and Stockholm. Six Coop stores in Gästrikland and Hälsingland were affected, but the full number of Swedish stores involved remained unclear.

The ICA store in Sjöbo temporarily closed after reporting temperatures around 50°C. In Sankt Olof, store manager Dennis Vidal said workers were emptying freezers as cooling began to return, but the food was already ruined. At ICA Baronen in Stockholm, staff reported temperatures rising from 38°C to around 50°C.

ICA press officer Gustaf Nilsson said the company was investigating and helping affected stores. Importantly, ICA said the affected shops had connections outside its central network. That distinction does not establish how attackers gained access, but it means the incident should not automatically be described as a breach of ICA’s central systems.

The Swedish reports have not identified the controller brands, entry point, exploited software flaw or attackers. There is also no confirmed evidence that the same group targeted stores in Sweden and France. Any claim naming a specific vulnerability would therefore be premature.

However, the earlier French incidents show why connected cooling equipment needs close attention. Cybersecurity News previously reported on supermarket refrigerators being remotely manipulated, with attackers reportedly changing settings to keep equipment in defrost mode. This function normally clears ice, but prolonged operation can raise temperatures and destroy stock.

France’s national cyber response team, CERT-FR, confirmed compromises involving Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers, alongside Copeland xweb and Dixell xweb devices. Its official refrigeration security alert warned against exposing management interfaces directly to the internet. These findings concern the French incidents, not confirmed equipment at Swedish stores.

A related Cybersecurity News report on exposed Danfoss systems highlighted how widely refrigeration management pages could be reached online. Such exposure creates a direct route to equipment that controls physical conditions, rather than only business records or payment systems.

CERT-FR advises operators to remove public internet access, check controller settings, including defrost schedules, and restore remote access through a secure VPN or protected network. It also recommends firmware updates and changing default passwords. Operators should coordinate changes with refrigeration providers, including checking insurance terms before interrupting monitoring connections.

The agency also warns that resetting an unsupported controller is not enough. Without removing exposure and addressing the underlying weakness, the equipment can be compromised again, putting replacement stock at risk once cooling resumes and stores begin restocking their shelves.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Quick Answer: Linx is the AI-native solution for modern IGA across all identity types; SailPoint remains the IGA benchmark with AI-driven certifications; Saviynt leads cloud-native converged governance; Microsoft Entra ID Governance wins bundled economics in M365 estates; Omada owns the configurable mid-enterprise; One Identity rules AD-heavy shops.

IGA answers the question auditors always ask: who should have access and can you prove it?

Access reviews done in spreadsheets are how audit findings and insider breaches happen. Identity Governance & Administration automates the entitlement lifecycle: joiner-mover-leaver provisioning, access certifications, separation-of-duties enforcement, and the continuous evidence trail that SOX, ISO, and enterprise cybersecurity frameworks now expect on an ongoing basis rather than during annual scrambles.

The 2026 field pairs deep incumbents with cloud-native challengers, while AI-assisted certification (recommend, don’t rubber-stamp) became the real differentiator.

We scored ten tools across five weighted criteria, then detail each features, best fit, pros, cons. Editorial assessment, not a lab test; pricing by model only.

Table of Contents

  1. How We Evaluated
  2. The Scorecard
  3. The 10 Tools in Depth
  4. Full Comparison Table
  5. Buyer’s Guide
  6. FAQ

How We Evaluated the Best Identity Governance & Administration (IGA) Tools in 2026

To select the top 10 Identity Governance and Administration (IGA) tools in 2026, we evaluated each solution based on its identity security capabilities, governance features, automation, scalability, and overall business value. Our evaluation focuses on the following 10 key criteria:

1. Identity Lifecycle Management: We assess how effectively each tool automates user provisioning, access modifications, and deprovisioning across employee, contractor, and third-party identities.

2. Access Governance and Certification: We evaluate access reviews, periodic certifications, entitlement management, and approval workflows to determine how well organizations can control user permissions.

3. Role-Based Access Control (RBAC): We examine how each platform supports role management, least-privilege access, role mining, and separation of duties (SoD) to reduce unnecessary access.

4. Automation and AI Capabilities: We assess AI-driven access recommendations, automated identity workflows, risk-based decisions, and intelligent access reviews that reduce manual administrative work.

5. Integration and Compatibility: We examine integration capabilities with Active Directory, Microsoft Entra ID, cloud applications, HR systems, enterprise applications, and existing security infrastructure.

6. Compliance and Audit Readiness: We evaluate built-in reporting, audit trails, access certification records, and support for regulatory requirements such as GDPR, HIPAA, SOX, and ISO 27001.

7. Security and Risk Management: We assess how effectively each solution detects excessive privileges, orphaned accounts, toxic access combinations, and identity-related security risks.

8. Scalability and Deployment Flexibility: We examine whether the platform supports growing enterprise environments, hybrid infrastructures, multi-cloud deployments, and complex organizational structures.

9. Ease of Use and Administration: We evaluate dashboard usability, configuration complexity, workflow customization, deployment effort, and the administrative skills required for ongoing management.

10. Pricing, Support, and Overall Value: We consider licensing models, implementation costs, technical support, documentation, customer feedback, and the overall value delivered to organizations of different sizes.

Our Evaluation Approach: These criteria provide a consistent framework for comparing IGA solutions based on security effectiveness, operational efficiency, and enterprise requirements. The final ranking should also consider verified product documentation, available demonstrations, independent user reviews, and publicly documented capabilities to help organizations identify the most suitable identity governance platform for their needs.

The Scorecard

The 10 Tools in Depth

1. Linx Security

Description. The AI-native leader: Linx is the identity security platform for the agentic era. Linx’s AI-native platform unifies identity discovery, posture management, and access governance to help organizations uncover critical exposures, prioritize what matters most, and enforce least-privilege access.

From employees and service accounts to applications and AI agents, Linx enables organizations to govern every identity and proactively mitigate risk across the enterprise.

Key features: Autonomous agents; identity graph; lifecycle automation; access review campaigns; MCP Gateway; converged IGA+ISPM

Best for: Mid-market and enterprise teams modernizing IGA that don’t want to rely on professional services

Pros: AI-driven review automation; unified governance and posture; native NHI and AI agent coverage; time-to-value.

Cons: Newer vendor with a smaller install base.

2. Saviynt

Description. The cloud-native converger: Enterprise Identity Cloud delivers converged IGA and Cloud Infrastructure Entitlement Management (CIEM) alongside application GRC in a single unified SaaS platform strongest where governance must bridge SaaS applications, multi-cloud control planes, and SAP-grade SoD without deploying three separate products.

Key features: Converged IGA+CIEM+app GRC; fine-grained SoD (SAP/ERP depth); cloud-native SaaS; risk-based certifications; peer analytics.

Best for: Cloud-first enterprises and ERP-heavy compliance.

Pros: Convergence breadth; ERP SoD depth; SaaS delivery.

Cons: Configuration complexity at depth; services-heavy deployments persist.

3. Microsoft (Entra ID Governance)

Description. Governance at bundle economics: native entitlement management, access reviews, lifecycle workflows, and Privileged Identity Management (PIM) integration built directly into Microsoft Entra hardening directories to prevent scenarios where Microsoft Entra ID vulnerabilities let attackers escalate privilegesthrough unmonitored service principals and federated roles.

Key features: Access packages/entitlement management; automated access reviews; lifecycle workflows (JML); PIM synergy; published add-on pricing.

Best for: M365 estates wanting governance without a new platform.

Pros: Price/level of effort unbeatable in-stack; native depth.

Cons: Cross-platform/legacy connector breadth trails specialists; deep SoD lighter than SailPoint/Saviynt.

4. One Identity (Identity Manager)

Description. The Active Directory and SAP workhorse: Identity Manager delivers granular lifecycle provisioning, access certification, and SoD policy enforcement, supported by active vendor patches that remediate One Identity Manager privilege escalation vulnerabilities
across on-premises enterprise environments.

Key features: Deep AD/SAP connectors; granular lifecycle; certification/SoD; data governance extension; on-prem/hybrid deployment.

Best for: AD/SAP-centric enterprises modernizing deliberately.

Pros: AD/SAP depth benchmark; deployment control.

Cons: Cloud-native polish trails SaaS rivals; interface utilitarian.

5. IBM (Verify Governance)

Description. Governance with services scale: IBM Verify Governance handles access certification, automated provisioning, and role and risk modeling, supported by security updates addressing vulnerabilities in the IBM Security Verify platform typically deployed inside larger IBM identity or GRC transformations where consulting delivery matters as much as software.

Key features: Certifications; provisioning; role/risk modeling; SAP integration; IBM services ecosystem.

Best for: IBM-aligned enterprises and services-led programs.

Pros: Enterprise credibility; services muscle.

Cons: Product momentum trails leaders; ecosystem-dependent value.

6. Omada

Description. The configurable mid-enterprise champion: Omada Identity Cloud incorporates standard IGA process frameworks (IdentityPROCESS+) that deploy in weeks rather than years, aligned with essential criteria for choosing the right enterprise IAM and IGA solutions to deliver European-grade governance globally.

Key features: Templated best-practice processes; certification/SoD; lifecycle automation; SaaS delivery; strong European compliance fit.

Best for: Mid-to-large enterprises wanting depth without SailPoint-scale programs.

Pros: Time-to-value with real depth; process templates.

Cons: Connector breadth and AI trail the top two; NA brand still building.

7. Oracle (Access Governance)

Description. Oracle-estate governance modernized: the cloud-native Access Governance service brings AI-assisted access reviews and continuous lifecycle automation across Oracle applications, OCI, and databases, protecting against configuration gaps that expose vulnerabilities in Oracle E-Business Suite and ERP applications.

Key features: AI-assisted access reviews; OCI-native service; Oracle app/DB connector depth; lifecycle; usage-based cloud pricing.

Best for: Oracle-centric enterprises.

Pros: Oracle-stack integration; modernized SaaS delivery.

Cons: Limited pull beyond Oracle estates; ecosystem breadth narrow.

8. Okta (Identity Governance)

Description. Governance unified where access lives: Okta Identity Governance (OIG) adds access requests, periodic certifications, and lifecycle workflows natively to Okta’s core platform, evaluated in our top identity and access management solutions roundup for SaaS-centric businesses.

Key features: Access requests/certifications in Okta; workflow automation; lifecycle synergy with Okta provisioning; per-user add-on pricing.

Best for: Okta estates needing pragmatic governance fast.

Pros: Zero-friction adoption; unified admin.

Cons: SoD/analytics depth trails specialists; Okta-tenant scope.

9. RSA (Governance & Lifecycle)

Description. The installed-base stalwart: RSA Governance & Lifecycle (formerly Aveksa) serves long-standing enterprise deployments with access certification, request management, and identity tracking, evaluated among enterprise user access management and governance tools
for high-assurance compliance.

Key features: Certifications; lifecycle; violation management; on-prem strength; RSA Unified Identity platform alignment.

Best for: Existing RSA governance estates optimizing continuity.

Pros: Proven at scale; incumbent stability.

Cons: New-selection momentum low; modernization diligence needed.

10. Ping Identity (incl. ForgeRock)

Description. Scope note: Ping Identity (with ForgeRock unified under its umbrella) is primarily an access management and CIAM platform; its governance capabilities focus on identity orchestration and relationship modeling aligned with NIST Zero Trust Architecture guidelines
, typically pairing with a specialist like SailPoint or Saviynt for full SoD programs.

Key features: Identity lifecycle (ForgeRock lineage); relationship/role modeling; orchestration hooks to IGA partners; unified Ping platform.

Best for: Ping-anchored estates with light governance needs or as the access layer beside specialist IGA.

Pros: Orchestration strength; platform consolidation.

Cons: Not a certification/SoD specialist; pair for full IGA.

Full Comparison Table

Buyer’s Guide

Match program appetite to platform weight. Full-scale regulated governance → SailPoint (depth/AI) or Saviynt (convergence/ERP). Weeks-not-years with real depth → Omada.

M365-centric → Entra ID Governance first; add a specialist only where its SoD/connector gaps bite. Okta-centric SaaS estates → OIG for pragmatic coverage. AD/SAP-on-prem truth → One Identity. Oracle estates → Access Governance.

AI is the certification cure: recommendation engines (SailPoint’s benchmark) are what stop reviewers from approve-all fatigue demand live demos on your entitlement data.

Secure on-premises truth: Where Active Directory and legacy on-premises systems remain authoritative, One Identity provides direct operational control ensure environments are audited against an Active Directory security checklist to eliminate stale privileged accounts.

Key takeaways: per-identity quoting dominates (Entra’s published add-on is the price anchor); machine and non-employee identities are the growth audit surface verify coverage; convergence (Saviynt IGA+CIEM) saves platforms but adds configuration; and certification evidence must export cleanly auditors, not dashboards, are the customer.

FAQ

What are the best IGA tools in 2026?

SailPoint (benchmark depth/AI), Saviynt (cloud-native convergence), Entra ID Governance (bundled economics), Omada (configurable time-to-value), One Identity (AD/SAP depth) with Okta OIG, Oracle, IBM, and RSA serving their ecosystems.

What does IGA do that IAM doesn’t?

IAM authenticates and connects users; IGA governs entitlements automated joiner-mover-leaver provisioning, access certifications, SoD enforcement, and audit evidence. IAM is the door; IGA decides who deserves keys.

How is IGA priced?

Per governed identity per year, almost universally by quote SailPoint/Saviynt/Omada at premium tiers, with Microsoft’s published Entra ID Governance add-on the market’s transparent price anchor, and Okta OIG a per-user add-on.

Why is IGA critical for preventing privilege abuse?

Unmonitored entitlement creep leaves orphaned accounts and dormant permissions open for attackers. Understanding how attackers exploit privileged access highlights why continuous access certifications and automated deprovisioning are necessary to starve lateral movement.

SailPoint or Saviynt?

SailPoint for the deepest certifications, AI, and connector maturity; Saviynt for converged IGA+CIEM+ERP GRC in one SaaS. ERP-heavy SoD leans Saviynt; broadest governance depth leans SailPoint. Both are program commitments.

Is Entra ID Governance enough?

For M365-centric estates with moderate SoD needs often yes, at unbeatable economics. Cross-platform connector depth, ERP SoD, and advanced role mining remain the specialist’s territory.

Why did AI become the IGA differentiator?

Certification fatigue: reviewers rubber-stamp bulk approvals. AI recommendations, peer-group outliers, and role mining turn reviews into risk decisions measurably reducing inappropriate access instead of documenting it.

Conclusion

IGA turns “who has access” from an audit scramble into an automated, evidenced process. SailPoint sets the depth-and-AI benchmark; Saviynt converges governance with cloud entitlements; Entra ID Governance makes M365 estates governance-credible at add-on pricing; Omada compresses time-to-value; One Identity, Oracle, IBM, RSA, and Okta serve their strongholds; and Ping (ForgeRock) plays the access layer beside true specialists.

Demand AI recommendations on your own data, verify machine-identity coverage, and buy the platform your program appetite can actually feed.
