articles.title: Zero-Click ‘SMS of Death’ Flaw Lets Hackers Disrupt Android Phones With a Single Text
articles.description:
A security researcher has published details of a zero-click Android flaw called “SMS of Death.” One malformed text message can crash the phone service on an Android device, drop active calls, and in the worst case leave the phone without telephony after every restart. Google has marked the report “Won’t Fix” and treats it as […]

The post Zero-Click ‘SMS of Death’ Flaw Lets Hackers Disrupt Android Phones With a Single Text appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A security researcher has published details of a zero-click Android flaw called “SMS of Death.” One malformed text message can crash the phone service on an Android device, drop active calls, and in the worst case leave the phone without telephony after every restart. Google has marked the report “Won’t Fix” and treats it as a non-security issue, according to the researcher’s disclosure site.

The bug sits in WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu(), the Android code that reads WAP Push messages. These are special data texts that never show up in the inbox. The code reads a header length from the message as a long number and then converts it to a smaller signed integer without checking the range.

The researcher shows that the five bytes 88 80 80 80 00 turn into -2147483648 after this conversion. Android then tries to create a byte array of that size.

That throws an uncaught NegativeArraySizeException and kills the com.android.phone process. The victim sees nothing. No message appears, and the sender’s number stays hidden.

Zero-Click ‘SMS of Death’ Flaw

Active calls end with the cause CS_DEATH as the process restarts. Each message causes one to two seconds without service. The carrier also resends texts the phone never acknowledges, so one message caused repeated outages for up to a week in testing.

About 20 messages left a phone unusable for a long time. The researcher tested a Pixel 9 on April 2026 firmware, and several Samsung Galaxy and A-series phones, and the crash happened every time.

Android already has other zero-click risks from fake cell towers. Google’s Android 17 adds protections against 2G downgrade and SMS blaster tricks. Those protections target a different problem and do not appear to cover this parsing bug.

Sending about 30 messages in quick succession is far worse. The repeated crashes collide with writes to the SMS store and corrupt the SQLite database that holds messages. After that, the phone app crashes on every boot, and a restart does not help.

A factory reset only works for a short time, because the carrier sends the stuck payload again. The researcher’s fix was to move the physical SIM into a non-Android phone such as an iPhone so the carrier’s retries get acknowledged. Then the corrupt records had to be cleared over ADB. An eSIM would make recovery much harder, and most users could not do it.

Zero-click attacks on phones are not new. In 2023, Citizen Lab found BLASTPASS, an iPhone zero-click chain used to install Pegasus spyware

AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

The post AppViewX Expands Quantum Trust Hub with Cryptographic Discovery, Posture Management, and Remediation appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
New York, New York, October 29th, 2026, CyberNewswire

Now available as a standalone solution, Quantum Trust Hub delivers cryptographic posture management and agility for enterprises to uncover risk exposure, drive remediation at scale, and accelerate quantum readiness.  

AppViewX, the leading identity security company built for the AI-powered and post-quantum enterprise, today announced new capabilities for Quantum Trust Hub, now available as a standalone solution to help enterprises discover cryptographic assets, assess quantum-related vulnerabilities, prioritize risks by business impact, and take decisive action through integrated remediation workflows.

The new capabilities include an agentless-first approach that leverages organizations’ existing security infrastructure to discover cryptographic assets without the additional overhead of agents and sensors.

Organizations can also upload Cryptographic Bills of Materials (CBOMs) and Software Bills of Materials (SBOMs) from third-party tools to build a single, unified inventory of cryptographic assets, and initiate remediation planning and execution through existing ITSM solutions.  

As enterprises prepare for the transition to post-quantum cryptography (PQC), understanding where vulnerable cryptography exists across their environments is becoming increasingly critical.

NIST finalized its first PQC standards in 2024 and has outlined plans to begin phasing out RSA and ECC in 2030.

By that same year, Executive Order 14412 directs federal agencies to transition high-value assets and high-impact systems to PQC for key establishment, with PQC adoption for digital signatures to follow by the end of 2031.

Meeting these deadlines requires a comprehensive understanding of cryptographic exposure, yet traditional certificate inventories alone do not tell the full story.

Cryptographic exposure extends beyond certificates to TLS configurations, keys, and application code, making it difficult to assess true risk and know where to focus first. 

Addressing these challenges requires continuous visibility across multiple layers of cryptographic infrastructure. Quantum Trust Hub delivers this through a vendor-neutral approach, consolidating findings from existing security tools and third-party inventories.

By building a unified cryptographic inventory and extending visibility across certificates, TLS configurations, cipher suites, and code libraries, the platform gives security teams the cryptographic posture management foundation they need, enabling continuous assessment of exposure, risk-based remediation prioritization, and the cryptographic agility to respond quickly as threats and standards evolve.  

“The quantum transition is a complex undertaking that enterprises need to start preparing for now,” said Jennifer Glenn, research director at IDC.

“Recent attacks involving compromised cryptographic credentials and signing keys underscore the risks organizations already face today. With federal migration deadlines approaching and quantum computing potentially advancing faster than expected, understanding the full scope of cryptographic exposure will be essential to planning an effective response.” 

With the latest Quantum Trust Hub capabilities, enterprises can: 

  • Expand cryptographic discovery using existing security investments: Through a new integration with Qualys, alongside existing Tenable support, organizations can discover cryptographic assets and configurations using security tools already deployed across their environments. AppViewX’s agentless-first approach reduces cost and complexity while supporting deeper discovery when needed.  
  • Build a single, unified cryptographic inventory: CBOMs and SBOMs from third-party tools can be uploaded directly into the platform, consolidating findings from multiple discovery sources across certificates, TLS configurations, cipher suites, keys, and application code. This provides the foundation for true cryptographic posture management. 
  • Prioritize what matters most: Assets are classified as quantum-vulnerable or quantum-resistant. Business application context and NIST-aligned severity ratings enable organizations to surface the most critical remediation priorities to address first. Executive dashboards and continuous monitoring track posture and migration progress over time. 
  • Drive remediation through existing ITSM workflows: Cryptographic findings are sent directly to ServiceNow as ready-to-work tickets containing affected assets, identified risks, recommended fixes, and ownership information. Tickets are grouped by remediation scope, with status tracked end-to-end so teams can ensure findings translate into action, not just reports. 
  • Move faster with cryptographic agility: By maintaining a comprehensive, continuously updated inventory of cryptographic assets and their risk status, organizations can respond quickly to new vulnerabilities, policy changes, and evolving PQC standards, without having to scramble to understand their exposure from scratch. 

The expansion of Quantum Trust Hub reinforces AppViewX’s broader mission to secure machine and AI identities, credentials, and cryptography through a cohesive product portfolio as enterprises navigate the transition to post-quantum computing.

Quantum Trust Hub works alongside AppViewX’s CLM and SSH Key Lifecycle Management solutions to accelerate remediation of certificates or SSH keys that require replacement as part of a PQC assessment.

Additionally, AppViewX recently advanced its Agent Identity Security solution to discover, govern, and control the actions of AI agents at runtime while extending its core CLM and PKI products to issue cryptographically verifiable, quantum-resilient identities for AI agents, establishing an additional layer of trust as they access enterprise systems.

Together, these offerings provide enterprises with a more comprehensive approach to securing machine and agent identities while managing cryptographic risk across their environments.  

“The quantum clock is ticking, and enterprises cannot afford to wait until post-quantum migration becomes an immediate requirement to understand their exposure,” said Archit Lohokare, CEO of AppViewX.

“Certificates are only one part of the equation. Cryptographic risk extends across the identities, keys, protocols, and applications that underpin enterprise trust. With Quantum Trust Hub, we’re giving organizations the continuous visibility and risk intelligence needed to identify vulnerable cryptography, focus on their most critical exposures, and take a more proactive approach to quantum readiness.” 

To learn more about Quantum Trust Hub, watch AppViewX’s on-demand webinar, “The Quantum Readiness Clock Is Ticking: What to Do Now” or explore a 30-day quantum readiness assessment by talking to an AppViewX expert. 

About AppViewX    

AppViewX is the leading machine and agent identity security company built for the AI and quantum enterprise, bringing together discovery, automation, control, and intelligence.

The AVX Platform helps enterprises reduce risk by providing complete visibility and governance over every machine and AI agent identity, automating their lifecycle, controlling their access, and ensuring compliance at the speed business demands.   

Trusted by global enterprises across financial services, healthcare, and technology, AppViewX is recognized as a leader in the IDC MarketScape for Certificate Lifecycle Management and KuppingerCole’s Non-Human Identity Management Leadership Compass. For more information, users can visit appviewx.com.

articles.description:

It carries a CVSS score of 10.0 and lets a remote attacker skip authentication and gain administrative rights without a password. KeyDrift is built to sit quietly […]

The post Hackers Exploit Critical Cisco SD-WAN 0-Day Flaw to Deploy KeyDrift Malware and Steal Encryption Keys appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A state-linked hacking group used a maximum-severity Cisco SD-WAN zero-day flaw to break into network controllers and install a custom malware framework called KeyDrift.

The flaw is CVE-2026-20127. It carries a CVSS score of 10.0 and lets a remote attacker skip authentication and gain administrative rights without a password.

KeyDrift is built to sit quietly inside the control system of a Cisco SD-WAN network. It copies the keys that protect traffic between company sites, and it also works as a backdoor.

The targets named so far include space and satellite services, defense and aerospace companies, and policy research groups. Researchers from Cisco Talos identified the malware and published their findings on October 28, 2026.

Talos tracks the actor as UAT-11473 and calls it a highly sophisticated advanced persistent threat (APT) group. It describes the activity as historical. It does not say when the intrusions happened or whether any stolen keys were actually sent out.

Hackers Exploit Critical Cisco SD-WAN 0-Day Flaw

The flaw sits in the peering authentication of the Catalyst SD-WAN Controller, Manager and Validator. An attacker sends crafted requests and logs in as a high-privileged internal user, which opens the door to NETCONF and lets them change the network setup.

Cisco says no workaround exists, so patching is the only fix. Researchers later published a public proof-of-concept exploit for the same bug, which raised the risk for unpatched systems.

After getting in, the attackers edit the startup scripts, known as runit service paths, so the malware starts with normal services. A script named conf_sshd finds the running vdaemon processes, and a tool called rsshd injects the main module into each one.

That module is PolyFlame. It lives only in memory and acts as a backdoor that can run commands and read or write files. It can also relay orders to other infected machines. One variant pretends to be the legitimate aaamgr service and uses anti-debugging checks to hide.

The second module, LittleFilch, does the key theft. It hooks a function called SSL_read inside vdaemon and reads control messages after they are decrypted.

For a preset list of edge routers, it grabs IP addresses and a 32-byte field that Talos believes is AES-256 key material for IPsec traffic.

LittleFilch encrypts the haul with RSA, saves it to a file, and can send it out over UDP to an address in a config file that it deletes after reading.

Links to Volt Typhoon and How to Defend

Talos says with high confidence that UAT-11473’s infrastructure overlaps heavily with “Silent Train,” a covert access network linked to Volt Typhoon.

That group has a record of hijacking routers, and earlier reporting on Volt Typhoon targeting Cisco routers shows how it turns edge devices into hidden relay points.

Cisco fixed CVE-2026-20127 in February 2026, so the first step is to confirm every controller runs a patched build. The first fixed releases are 20.9.8.2, 20.12.6.1, 20.15.4.2 and 20.18.2.1, depending on your release train.

Versions older than 20.9 must move to a supported release. Until you upgrade, limit ports 22 and 830 to known controller addresses, but remember this does not remove malware that is already there.

Patching alone is not enough if you were exposed earlier. Check /var/log/auth.log for “Accepted publickey for vmanage-admin” entries from unknown IP addresses, and look for the files listed below.

Run “request admin-tech” on each control component before opening a Cisco TAC case. Defenders should also watch for a newer SD-WAN Controller flaw, CVE-2026-20182, which uses the same vdaemon service and was also exploited. For full guidance, see the Cisco security advisory.

articles.title: Chinese Hackers Use Secret Silent Train Network to Exploit Zero-Days Against U.S. Government and Defense
articles.description:
China-linked Volt Typhoon hackers have used a covert network called Silent Train to hide zero-day attacks against U.S. government agencies, defense contractors and critical infrastructure. The network chains together compromised routers, connected devices and enterprise servers, helping operators reach sensitive systems while concealing where their activity begins. The investigation connects years of carefully targeted intrusions […]

The post Chinese Hackers Use Secret Silent Train Network to Exploit Zero-Days Against U.S. Government and Defense appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
China-linked Volt Typhoon hackers have used a covert network called Silent Train to hide zero-day attacks against U.S. government agencies, defense contractors and critical infrastructure.

The network chains together compromised routers, connected devices and enterprise servers, helping operators reach sensitive systems while concealing where their activity begins.

The investigation connects years of carefully targeted intrusions to attacks on centralized management platforms.

These systems already hold trusted access to large networks, allowing attackers to steal credentials and reach customer environments without repeatedly breaking into individual machines.

Researchers from Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs identified and tracked Silent Train over three years, issuing hundreds of victim notifications.

Their October 28 report describes four confirmed zero-day campaigns and one likely campaign. Silent Train is an operational framework, not a single malware family; investigations also uncovered malicious in-memory webshells.

Chinese Hackers Use Secret Silent Train Network

First observed in November 2023, Silent Train grew as Volt Typhoon moved beyond its disrupted KV-botnet infrastructure.

Earlier reporting on Volt Typhoon router exploitation documented the group’s use of compromised networking equipment as covert relays, but Lumen describes a more disposable and tightly controlled operating model.

Sessions start on virtual private servers outside the United States, pass through compromised overseas devices, then enter U.S.-based infrastructure before reaching victims.

Domestic exit points help traffic appear less suspicious and evade geographic restrictions. Some operations placed as many as six intermediary hops between the operator and target.

Lumen observed more than 27 device classes, including TP-Link routers, Netgear Orbi devices, Fortinet appliances and CyberPanel servers.

Operators exploited exposed web interfaces and installed temporary SSH services, keys and configuration files. Chains could be assembled in under two minutes, while sessions averaged about four hours. Operators then removed their tools and dismantled the connections.

Device roles remained consistent: Intelbras modems appeared as overseas relays, while Netgear Orbi devices served as U.S. hops.

By early 2025, enterprise systems added longer-lived final connections that remained active for one to three months. Some sessions also used reverse tunnels instead of relying entirely on sequential SSH connections.

Activity also followed a human work pattern. Most sessions occurred Monday through Friday, between 09:00 and 22:00 China Standard Time, with less activity overnight and on weekends.

Individual sessions generally targeted one to five victims, often just one organization, underscoring the group’s selective use of the covert network.

Management Platforms Give Attackers Wider Access

The targets explain the value of this hidden infrastructure. Endpoint managers and software-defined wide-area network controllers provide device inventories, credentials and administrative functions.

Previous coverage of exposed N-central management servers highlighted how weaknesses in one platform can threaten managed service providers and customers. Lumen linked Silent Train activity to exploitation of two previously undisclosed N-central vulnerabilities.

Other campaigns targeted Versa Director, Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN and VeloCloud Orchestrator. Versa intrusions involved an in-memory JAR webshell that reduced evidence on disk.

Cisco activity targeted trusted peering mechanisms, while VeloCloud became the third SD-WAN platform exploited through Silent Train.

A separate Quest KACE campaign affected more than 30 victims, although limited logs prevented researchers from identifying the underlying flaw.

Lumen assessed the KACE zero-day link with moderate confidence, noting that activity declined after October 2025 security updates.

That distinction matters: not every observed intrusion proves an unknown vulnerability was used, and the researchers could not determine the access method for every targeted product.

The findings also extend earlier reporting on Cisco SD-WAN zero-day exploitation by showing Volt Typhoon using the affected control plane by late 2025 and continuing after disclosure in February 2026.

Across campaigns, attackers harvested credentials, abused remote administration and file-transfer features, and sometimes altered or erased logs.

Hawaii, California and Texas repeatedly emerged as targeting hotspots. Victims included telecommunications companies, satellite communications providers, universities with defense ties and essential service operators.

Lumen considers the pattern consistent with positioning access inside networks supporting U.S. operations, particularly during Indo-Pacific crises, rather than evidence that disruption has already occurred.

Defenders should restrict internet-facing management interfaces, prioritize vendor patches and review downstream trust relationships.

Lumen also recommends exporting logs, extending retention and investigating unusual administrative activity, API requests, remote transfers and configuration changes. External logging is particularly important when attackers can erase evidence on the compromised platform.

articles.title: Hackers Claim Wagyu Crypto Platform Breach as Researchers Find Thousands of Monero Transaction Records
articles.description:
Hackers have claimed a breach of cryptocurrency swap platform Wagyu.xyz, while researchers reviewing the purported leak found thousands of records connecting Monero transactions with public blockchain payments and IP addresses. The dataset contains 38,628 order records and 10,139 distinct IP addresses, covering activity between July 18 and October 26, 2026. Its origin and authenticity remain […]

The post Hackers Claim Wagyu Crypto Platform Breach as Researchers Find Thousands of Monero Transaction Records appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers have claimed a breach of cryptocurrency swap platform Wagyu.xyz, while researchers reviewing the purported leak found thousands of records connecting Monero transactions with public blockchain payments and IP addresses.

The dataset contains 38,628 order records and 10,139 distinct IP addresses, covering activity between July 18 and October 26, 2026. Its origin and authenticity remain independently unverified.

The findings highlight a privacy risk beyond cryptocurrency code: information held by services that move funds between blockchains. Unlike a wallet compromise, a transaction database leak can expose financial relationships without revealing private keys.

The earlier Coinbase customer data breach similarly showed how exposed account information could create social-engineering risks without directly compromising customer funds.

Researchers from Infostealers, Hudson Rock’s threat-intelligence publication, reported their findings on October 28. They noted that infostealer malware can expose credentials, browser activity and cryptocurrency information, but found no evidence that such malware caused this alleged incident or infected identified Wagyu customers.

Hackers Claim Wagyu Crypto Platform Breach

Ransomware-tracking services indexed WhiteArmor-associated listings naming Wagyu on October 27–28, including an entry titled “wagyu.xyz unfairness.”

The accompanying claims focused on allegedly hidden swap fees and unfair coin-flip odds. However, a threat actor’s listing does not establish that ransomware was deployed, data was stolen, or financial misconduct occurred.

Hudson Rock examined an order export and a separate IP-level activity summary. Researchers identified 8,137 orders naming native Monero receiving addresses, including 6,692 marked completed.

Within the completed cross-chain subset, 4,580 records joined an incoming transaction hash, an XMR destination and a client IP address. That group included 1,011 Bitcoin-to-Monero orders.

This matters because a swap provider must know where to deliver purchased coins. Its database may therefore connect a visible Bitcoin deposit with a Monero receiving address, timestamp, browser information and session identifier.

These service-side records expose relationships that are not available through ordinary inspection of Monero’s blockchain. The wider risk involves combining separate sources of metadata.

As reporting on stolen credentials fueling breaches explains, infostealer logs can contain browser sessions and wallet information. Such material could provide additional investigative context, although Hudson Rock did not report matching Wagyu records against infected users or stolen credentials.

The records also show the reverse direction. Researchers found 11,317 native-XMR-input swap orders containing service deposit addresses and destinations for other assets.

Among them, 9,187 completed records retained outgoing transaction hashes. These links can reveal a service’s public-chain payouts, but not which private Monero wallet originally supplied its deposits.

Some transaction groups carried labels including “Poloniex Hacker,” “Theft” and “Tornado.Cash: 100 ETH.” Six completed withdrawals labeled “Poloniex Hacker” totaled $1,025,047 in recorded value.

These are unverified database labels, not confirmed criminal attributions. Recorded amounts also do not establish stolen proceeds, and overlapping groups cannot be added into a reliable laundering total.

Privacy Risks, Data Retention and User Protection

The research does not demonstrate a weakness in Monero’s cryptography. Instead, it shows how information stored outside the blockchain can connect transaction requests and network activity.

An IP address is not a verified identity: VPNs, Tor, shared networks and automated services can represent several users, while one person may use multiple addresses.

Another concern involves 4,002 completed orders containing a populated userDeletedAt field. All retained an IP address and destination, while 3,180 also retained deposit transaction hashes.

The field alone cannot establish what users deleted, whether backups were involved, or whether Wagyu breached any retention promise or legal obligation.

If authentic, the records could support convincing refund scams, fake support messages or extortion attempts referencing real trades.

Separate campaigns using fake crypto wallet screens demonstrate why users should never enter recovery phrases into unexpected prompts. Hudson Rock did not establish that anyone had exploited the alleged Wagyu leak this way.

Users should verify notices through trusted channels and reject requests for private keys. Platforms should limit retention, restrict database access and explain how deletion affects logs and backups.

articles.title: Hackers Attack FreePBX Servers With Malware to Steal SIP Credentials for Phone Fraud
articles.description:
Hackers targeting FreePBX phone servers have upgraded their malware to steal credentials that can keep phone fraud running even after an infected system is rebuilt. The INJ3CTOR3 operation now collects configuration files containing SIP trunk passwords, database credentials, management secrets, and mail relay logins, extending the damage beyond the compromised server. The change builds on […]

The post Hackers Attack FreePBX Servers With Malware to Steal SIP Credentials for Phone Fraud appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers targeting FreePBX phone servers have upgraded their malware to steal credentials that can keep phone fraud running even after an infected system is rebuilt.

The INJ3CTOR3 operation now collects configuration files containing SIP trunk passwords, database credentials, management secrets, and mail relay logins, extending the damage beyond the compromised server.

The change builds on an earlier campaign that placed unauthorized calls through victims’ own phone systems.

Previously documented six-layer FreePBX persistence mechanisms helped the malware survive removal attempts, but stolen carrier credentials now give attackers another way to charge calls to a victim’s account.

Researchers from Cyble Research & Intelligence Labs identified the updated malware while examining artifacts collected from the operation’s staging servers in September 2026.

Their October 28 analysis describes an installer configured to upload 17 files repeatedly. Researchers recovered the upload commands but did not capture live exfiltration or establish a victim count.

Hackers Attack FreePBX Servers With Malware

The updated installer contains two encoded command groups, each directing configuration uploads to a separate staging server. Scheduled tasks run the installer every minute, repeatedly exposing secrets while the infection remains active.

Changing passwords before removing the malware can therefore hand replacement credentials straight back to the attacker. The targeted files span FreePBX, Issabel, Elastix, Asterisk, and Postfix configurations.

They include SIP and PJSIP authentication settings, Asterisk Manager Interface credentials, database passwords, and outbound mail authentication details. These files expose both calling services and supporting infrastructure.

SIP trunk credentials are particularly valuable because they authenticate a business’s connection to its telephone provider.

Unless the carrier restricts access to approved IP addresses, stolen credentials can let attackers register from another machine and place calls without using the original PBX. Those calls may leave no records on the cleaned server.

The operation retains its JOMANGY and ZenharR webshells, which provide remote commands and access to phone-system functions.

Related FreePBX webshell exploitation activity previously demonstrated how attackers combine administrative access, backdoor accounts, and outbound calling capabilities to monetize compromised VoIP infrastructure.

Cyble also found changes designed to weaken older detection rules. Webshell watermarks now vary between builds, and the password-gate hash has changed.

The underlying persistence remains largely unchanged, including scheduled downloads, login triggers, protected backup files, and multiple webshell copies that can restore deleted components.

Detection and Recovery Must Include Credential Rotation

Investigators should not treat a normal-looking FreePBX dashboard as proof that a server is clean. In laboratory testing, Cyble created an Asterisk trunk directly in configuration files that carried calls without appearing in the FreePBX console. Researchers did not observe this campaign planting such a trunk.

The malware also modifies web-server rewrite rules so requests containing encoded whitespace can reach a webshell without naming its file in access logs.

Meanwhile, the takeover script clears logs and command histories, reducing the evidence available for incident reconstruction. Recovery requires isolation, evidence preservation, and removal of persistence before rotation of exposed credentials.

Earlier guidance covering FreePBX zero-day server compromises similarly recommends clean restoration and replacement of system, trunk, extension, and other account secrets rather than relying on patching alone.

Administrators should coordinate with carriers to replace trunk secrets, preserve registration and billing records, restrict allowed source addresses, and set spending limits where available.

Monitoring should cover unexpected registrations, premium-rate destinations, unusual call concurrency, and outbound configuration uploads. Cyble recommends rebuilding from a trusted image as the most reliable recovery option.

articles.title: GitHub Launches Copilot Fusion for Smarter and Cheaper AI Coding
articles.description:
GitHub has launched Copilot Fusion, a system that automatically selects AI models for coding tasks, helping developers balance code quality, speed, and cost. Instead of choosing a model for every request, users select Fusion and let it decide how to handle the work. It is generally available in Visual Studio Code, Copilot CLI, the GitHub […]

The post GitHub Launches Copilot Fusion for Smarter and Cheaper AI Coding appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
GitHub has launched Copilot Fusion, a system that automatically selects AI models for coding tasks, helping developers balance code quality, speed, and cost.

Instead of choosing a model for every request, users select Fusion and let it decide how to handle the work. It is generally available in Visual Studio Code, Copilot CLI, the GitHub Copilot app, and JetBrains IDEs.

Fusion is a model router and coordinator, not a new standalone model. It checks each request for reasoning, code generation, debugging, and tool needs, then chooses the models and steps needed to produce one final answer. It also considers system health and model availability when making those choices.

Fusion uses three execution patterns. In Single mode, one model completes the task. Cascade starts with an efficient model, then uses a judge to inspect the draft and decide whether a stronger model should take over.

Critique sends a draft to several models for independent reviews before the original model revises its answer using their combined feedback.

These patterns can change within the same conversation. A simple request may use one model, while a difficult follow-up may trigger extra review.

GitHub Launches Copilot Fusion

GitHub says choosing a pattern adds little delay, although Cascade and Critique take longer because they involve additional model calls. Developers can follow progress and inspect which models contributed to the final response.

Fusion Standard selects one model for everyday work. Fusion High supports larger, clearly defined tasks, including difficult bug fixes and changes across several files.

Fusion Max targets work needing deeper reasoning. Fusion Fast serves speed-sensitive requests in Visual Studio Code inline chat and cannot be selected directly by users.

According to GitHub’s documentation, paid Copilot users get a 30% discount on Fusion model costs through November 30, 2026, though High and Max can consume more AI credits than Standard.

Fusion keeps the main conversation on the same model where possible to preserve cached tokens. Supporting models receive only the context they need.

Model selection also follows subscription limits, administrator restrictions, data residency rules, and FedRAMP requirements. Supported local models can participate through Fusion Standard in a public preview.

Extra AI review should not be mistaken for a security guarantee. Earlier reporting on GitHub Copilot prompt injection and the RoguePilot repository takeover flaw shows why untrusted project content remains a concern. Both issues were patched, and neither report establishes a vulnerability in Fusion.

GitHub also warns that discarding a draft does not automatically undo file edits that draft already made. Developers must review workspace changes before committing them. Fusion works separately from subagents and doesn’t launch them, so its role is coordination rather than independent agent management.

articles.description:
Microsoft urged Entra ID administrators to migrate from SMS and voice authentication in Entra ID to passkeys before retirement begins on February 1, 2027, to reduce phishing risks and prevent sign-in disruptions. The reminder, published on October 27 under Message Center notice MC1528000, follows July announcements. Retirement covers Worldwide and Government Community Cloud environments and […]

The post Microsoft Urges Entra ID Admins to Migrate from SMS and Voice Authentication to Passkeys appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft urged Entra ID administrators to migrate from SMS and voice authentication in Entra ID to passkeys before retirement begins on February 1, 2027, to reduce phishing risks and prevent sign-in disruptions.

The reminder, published on October 27 under Message Center notice MC1528000, follows July announcements. Retirement covers Worldwide and Government Community Cloud environments and should finish in early February 2027. Administrators should not wait until the change reaches their tenant before preparing affected users.

According to the Microsoft retirement notice, users with another registered sign-in method will use that method. They will not need to register a passkey to continue accessing their accounts. This makes checking existing authentication methods an important first step for administrators.

Users whose only registered method is SMS or voice face a different process. Microsoft says they can use their existing method one final time to verify their identity. They must then register a passkey to keep signing in, making preparation important for organizations with many phone-dependent accounts.

The announcement continues the shift covered in Cybersecuritynews.com’s report on Microsoft making passkeys the default in Entra ID. However, this retirement applies specifically to Microsoft-provided phone authentication, not a complete ban on SMS and voice across Entra ID.

Microsoft Urges Passkey Migration

SMS and voice authentication remain exposed to phishing and SIM-swap attacks. Criminals can trick users into sharing verification codes or take control of an authentication phone number. Moving away from these methods reduces reliance on phone networks and codes that attackers can capture.

As Microsoft’s passkey documentation explains, passkeys use public-key cryptography under FIDO standards. The user’s authenticator keeps the private key, while the service stores the public key. During sign-in, the authenticator signs a challenge after the user unlocks it with a PIN or biometric check.

The credential works only with the website or application it was created for, helping prevent fake login pages from stealing reusable sign-in secrets. Cybersecuritynews.com’s coverage of UNC3944’s SIM-swap attacks shows why reducing dependence on phone-based verification matters.

Administrators should identify users relying on SMS or voice, prioritize accounts without another registered method, and help users adopt passkeys or another supported option. Microsoft also asks organizations to notify employees and helpdesk teams about the deadline and the registration process.

Organizations that need to retain phone authentication can configure a customer-managed telecom provider through the Microsoft Security Store.

Microsoft’s provider guidance says configuration will be available starting October 30, 2026. Customers must review coverage, pricing, support, and contractual terms before deployment.

Existing customer-managed providers are unaffected. Organizations that do not use Microsoft-provided SMS or voice need no action for this retirement. At the same time, affected customers must migrate or configure their provider before February 1.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A network of 319 browser extensions has been linked to search hijacking affecting roughly 13.4 million users over a decade.

Marketed as PDF converters, manual finders, safe search tools, and AI search helpers, these extensions redirect queries through operator-controlled servers before sending users to Yahoo or Bing.

The business model turns ordinary searches into referral income while exposing queries to an intermediary. Similar behavior appeared in an earlier Chrome extension search hijacking investigation involving 23 add-ons, showing how basic browser settings can support large advertising operations.

Researchers from Socket.dev identified the extensions in an investigation published on October 29, 2026. Researcher John Tuckner reported 264 newly identified extensions affecting another 8.7 million users.

The headline figure combines findings across years; it does not establish that 13.4 million people remain actively affected today.

319 Chrome Extensions Found Hijacking Searches

The central technique abuses Chrome’s chrome_settings_overrides.search_provider setting, which lets an extension replace the default search engine.

One analyzed extension, Safe Game Search, contained only a manifest and three icons. It had no background worker, content scripts, toolbar interface, or requested permissions beyond its search configuration.

Chrome displays an installation prompt about changing search settings, but Socket said it does not clearly explain where queries ultimately travel.

This creates a detection gap: an extension can appear harmless during a permissions review while still placing an outside server between users and their search results.

Operators earn money through search syndication programs, which share advertising revenue with partners supplying traffic. Tracking parameters identify the partner receiving credit.

The additional proxy gives operators visibility into queries and control over each destination, rather than simply directing searches straight to a recognized search provider.

That differs from the broader capabilities documented in a fake GoogleTranslate Chrome extension case, where researchers found browser surveillance and remote interaction.

Here, the critical issue is narrower: search interception can happen without the invasive scripts or permissions usually associated with browser malware.

Predator Search illustrated the server-side control. Six identical queries produced four outcomes, including Yahoo results, alternative landing pages, an additional redirect chain, and an error page.

The extension itself never changed. Socket observed mostly referral-tagged search traffic, not confirmed phishing delivery, so malicious payload redirection remains a potential escalation rather than an established outcome.

The privacy risk extends beyond a changed homepage. Queries can reveal health concerns, financial problems, workplace projects, and personal interests.

Since the intermediary receives searches first, an otherwise familiar results page does not mean the request followed a direct or private route.

Hidden Distribution, Operator Links, and Defensive Checks

Most identified extensions were unlisted in the Chrome Web Store. Their pages remained accessible through direct links but did not appear in normal store searches.

Paid advertisements, including popovers and popunders, brought users to landing pages promoting apparently useful tools and encouraging installation.

The activity stretches back to 2016. Socket linked about 111 extensions and roughly 2.2 million installs to Intango LTD. Another cluster, SecuryBrowse, accounted for 58 extensions and approximately 4.9 million users.

A newer Bing-focused group contained 37 extensions, with coordinated updates across supposedly separate publishers providing evidence of shared operation.

Investigators combined store listings, privacy policies, Google Ads Transparency records, Censys, urlscan, and DecryptAds to connect landing pages and advertisers.

Shared advertising accounts and search partner tags helped reveal relationships that separate extension names and publisher branding could otherwise conceal.

Removal alone also has limits for investigators tracking the wider operation. Socket noted that domains can remain active after associated extensions disappear.

Following shared infrastructure and advertising relationships therefore provides a broader view than checking whether one individual store listing is still publicly available.

For defenders, the findings support checking search configuration alongside permissions. Earlier reporting on malicious Chrome extension infrastructure also highlighted the value of extension audits and managed allowlists.

Users should remove unfamiliar add-ons and verify their default search engine; organizations should investigate unexplained search redirects and restrict unapproved extensions.

articles.description:
A new exploit chain for Microsoft Edge revealed that combines five bugs and two Windows features to run code outside the browser sandbox. Published by Security researcher Orange Tsai on October 28, 2026, the research shows how flaws in browser logic can turn a malicious webpage into code execution on Windows without memory corruption. Tsai, […]

The post Microsoft Edge 0-Click Exploit Chains Five Flaws to Execute Code and Escape Sandbox appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A new exploit chain for Microsoft Edge revealed that combines five bugs and two Windows features to run code outside the browser sandbox.

Published by Security researcher Orange Tsai on October 28, 2026, the research shows how flaws in browser logic can turn a malicious webpage into code execution on Windows without memory corruption.

Tsai, a member of DEVCORE, built the chain for Pwn2Own Berlin 2026. His technical write-up describes two months of research completed without AI tools. The finished exploit used fewer than 100 lines of code.

The chain began in Edge’s Conditional Access navigation handler, which helps users switch to the right browser profile when accessing Microsoft services. When the supplied email matched the current profile, the handler started a new navigation using a supplied destination.

The crucial flaw was failing to bind that navigation to its original tab. Instead, Chromium used the active tab, letting JavaScript intended for one context run on another website. This created universal cross-site scripting, or UXSS, which breaks the boundary that normally keeps websites apart.

Microsoft Edge Zero-Click Exploit

Because the navigation came from the browser process, Tsai said that it could also bypass Content Security Policy protections. However, several checks still stood between this finding and an automatic attack.

First, Edge checked whether navigation came from a trusted Microsoft site, but failed to account for another window controlling that navigation. A cross-window flow bypassed this check. Separately, a hardcoded popup exception allowed the researcher to open a window without the usual user click.

The chain also needed a signed-in Edge profile and its email address. In the tested setup, Microsoft’s OneAuth feature could automatically create and sign in a profile using an existing Microsoft account when visiting a Microsoft website.

A cross-origin resource sharing misconfiguration on assets.msn.com then exposed the signed-in email to another website. Together, these steps removed the need for further clicks after attacker-controlled content loaded. The zero-click label therefore describes the automated chain, not an attack requiring no exposure to malicious web content.

Running JavaScript across websites was not enough to execute Windows code. Tsai next targeted Edge’s Immersive Reader, whose read:// address scheme was missing from the list blocking JavaScript URLs on privileged browser pages.

This exposed a native feedback function that packaged diagnostic logs. Path traversal and null-byte handling let the researcher write files outside the intended temporary folder and remove the enforced JSON extension. Cybersecurity News previously covered the related Edge feedback-log code execution vulnerability.

Tsai then changed protocols.json, an Edge configuration file controlling which websites may launch external protocol handlers. This allowed a webpage to invoke the Windows telnet handler. By placing a small executable in a writable directory Windows searches, he achieved code execution outside Edge’s sandbox.

Unlike the separately reported Edge memory-corruption vulnerability, this chain relied on logic errors and trusted features working together.

It shows why browser security reviews must test how navigation, identity, privileged pages, and Windows integrations interact, rather than checking each feature alone. Users should keep Edge updated through Microsoft’s security releases and avoid treating browser isolation as a complete defense.

articles.title: Hackers Use Fake Cloudflare Verification Pages to Target Windows and Mac Users
articles.description:
A new ClickFix campaign is using fake Cloudflare verification pages to trick both Windows and Mac users into running harmful commands on their own computers. The pages look like the “Verify you are human” checks that many people click through every day. Instead of a quick security check, the visitor ends up starting an infection […]

The post Hackers Use Fake Cloudflare Verification Pages to Target Windows and Mac Users appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A new ClickFix campaign is using fake Cloudflare verification pages to trick both Windows and Mac users into running harmful commands on their own computers.

The pages look like the “Verify you are human” checks that many people click through every day. Instead of a quick security check, the visitor ends up starting an infection by hand.

The campaign was seen on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, and it runs on legitimate websites that have been compromised. A visitor lands on a normal-looking site, and a hidden script loads the fake Cloudflare page on top of it.

Since the page shows different steps for each operating system, the trick works on Windows and macOS alike. It is a useful reminder that fake Cloudflare human check pages are still a favorite lure.

Researchers at the Internet Storm Center noted the activity. Handler Brad Duncan ran across it and published a diary entry titled “Yet Another ClickFix Campaign” on the SANS Internet Storm Center site.

Researcher said he had not seen this specific activity before and has not given it a name yet. He shared screenshots and indicators, and the full ISC diary is worth reading for the raw details.

Hackers Use Fake Cloudflare Verification Pages

The chain starts on the compromised website. A script loaded from the domain js-static[.]cfd runs in the visitor’s browser. Duncan saw the script call many paths on that domain, including ones that appear to check the visitor’s time zone, location and IP address.

It also loads a Cloudflare logo and fonts so the page looks real. This kind of tracking likely helps the attackers decide what to show each visitor, though the diary does not confirm that.

Next, the fake page tells the visitor to run a command to finish the “verification.” This is the core of ClickFix. No software flaw is used, and no file is downloaded.

The person does the risky step themselves, which helps the attack get past many security tools. Earlier reports on Windows and macOS users show the same split, where each system gets its own set of instructions.

In this case, Windows and Mac visitors saw different commands. The Windows command pointed to api-com[.]cfd, and the Mac command pointed to cf-id[.]com.

Duncan could not follow either one to the end. When he ran the Windows command, the server answered with a “403 Forbidden” error. On the Mac side, the domain did not resolve at all. As a result, the final malware for both systems is still unknown.

Duncan also removed the name of the compromised site from his report. He noted that searching for js-static[.]cfd in URLscan should turn up several other sites likely to produce the same traffic. That suggests the campaign is not limited to a single victim website.

Why ClickFix Keeps Working and How to Stay Safe

ClickFix keeps working because it uses trust instead of technical tricks. Most people know Cloudflare’s check and expect it to be harmless.

The fake version only adds one odd request, which is to paste something into Windows or Terminal. Many people follow a prompt like that without thinking, especially on a site they already know.

Other campaigns show how far this has spread. CERT-UA recently reported that more than 100 hacked sites pushed LUNEXSTEALER fake Cloudflare checks to Windows visitors.

Mac users are also targeted, and Apple has started to respond. Newer macOS versions now warn users with Apple’s Terminal paste protection when a suspicious command is pasted.

The best defense is a simple rule. A real Cloudflare check never asks you to open the Run box, PowerShell or Terminal. If a site asks for that, close the tab.

Companies can also block the Windows Run dialog through group policy, watch for odd PowerShell or Terminal activity, and block the domains listed below. Website owners should check their pages for unknown scripts, since the attackers rely on hacked sites to reach visitors.

articles.description:
Raw intelligence is cheap; operationalized intelligence is rare. A threat intelligence platform earns its keep by fusing feeds, deduplicating indicators, scoring relevance against your estate, and pushing enriched context into the SIEM, SOAR, and firewall before the analyst asks. The 2026 rankings reward platforms that close that loop, not those that merely aggregate. Recorded Future […]

The post Top 10 Best Threat Intelligence Platforms (TIP) in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Raw intelligence is cheap; operationalized intelligence is rare. A threat intelligence platform earns its keep by fusing feeds, deduplicating indicators, scoring relevance against your estate, and pushing enriched context into the SIEM, SOAR, and firewall before the analyst asks.

The 2026 rankings reward platforms that close that loop, not those that merely aggregate. Recorded Future takes 1; Anomali and ThreatConnect complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Recorded Future the intelligence graph with the broadest collection and cleanest productization.

• Podium: Recorded Future (collection breadth), Anomali (big-data intel analytics), ThreatConnect (intel-ops workflow).

• Buyer split: intelligence providers with platforms (Recorded Future, Mandiant, Flashpoint, Intel 471) versus neutral aggregation platforms (Anomali, ThreatQuotient, Cyware, EclecticIQ, ThreatConnect) many programs need one of each.

• 2026 theme: relevance scoring the TIP that ranks intel against your attack surface beats the one with the most feeds.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: collection/fusion breadth, relevance-scoring intelligence, operationalization depth (SIEM/SOAR/control push), analyst workbench quality, collaboration/sharing, and pricing accessibility.

Weights: operationalization 25%, collection/fusion 25%, relevance scoring 20%, workbench 15%, sharing 15%.

The 2026 TIP Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Recorded Future — Best Intelligence Graph & Collection

Snapshot: Module-based subscription | Intelligence Graph, 100+ sources classes | AI-assisted analyst tooling

Why it earns 1: Recorded Future industrialized intelligence: automated collection across open, technical, and dark sources into a graph that links actors, infrastructure, vulnerabilities, and targets, then packages it into modules a SOC can act on vulnerability prioritization, brand, geopolitical, identity exposure.

Its AI layer summarizes and drafts, cutting analyst reading time. The breadth comes at anchor-tier pricing.

Pros: Collection breadth; graph linkage; module productization; API depth.

Cons: Premium cost; module sprawl needs scoping discipline.

Bottom line: The most intelligence per query budget for it.

2. Anomali — Best Big-Data Intel Analytics

Snapshot: Platform tiers | ThreatStream TIP + Match retro-search | Copilot analytics

Why it ranks here: Anomali pairs a mature TIP (ThreatStream’s feed fusion, scoring, and dedup) with its differentiator: Match, which retro-searches years of your telemetry against fresh intel in seconds answering “were we already hit?” the moment an IOC publishes.

The big-data spine now powers broader security analytics ambitions.

Pros: Retro-matching at scale; feed-fusion maturity; analytics trajectory.

Cons: Full value assumes telemetry centralization.

Bottom line: The “were we already compromised?” machine.

3. OpenCTI (Filigran) — Best Open-Source Intel Operations Platform

Snapshot: Free Community + Enterprise | STIX 2.1 knowledge graph | Threat intelligence workflows + integrations

Why it ranks here: OpenCTI turns threat intelligence into a structured operational workflow by connecting indicators, threat actors, malware, vulnerabilities, campaigns, and TTPs inside a STIX 2.1-based knowledge graph.

It supports enrichment, case management, automation, intelligence sharing, and integrations with SIEM, SOAR, EDR, and other security tools, making it well suited for teams that want to build and operate a full threat intelligence function.

Pros: Open-source core; STIX 2.1 native; strong knowledge graph; broad connector ecosystem; case management and automation.

Cons: Self-hosting requires operational effort; some advanced capabilities and enterprise support require paid editions.

Bottom line: Build and operationalize threat intelligence around an open, structured knowledge graph.

4. Google (Mandiant) — Best Frontline Adversary Intel

Snapshot: Subscription tiers | Breach-frontline sourcing | Fused into Google SecOps

Why it ranks here: Mandiant’s edge is provenance: intelligence written by the teams inside the breaches, actor profiles with incident-floor grounding, and now native fusion into Google SecOps where fresh intel retro-hunts automatically.

As a neutral TIP it’s less the point; as an intelligence source with platform reach, it’s elite.

Pros: Frontline sourcing; actor-profile depth; SecOps fusion.

Cons: Platform story strongest inside Google’s suite.

Bottom line: The intel other intel cites.

5. Cyware — Best Intel Sharing & Collective Defense

Snapshot: Modular platform | CTIX TIP + CSAP sharing hub | ISAC/ISAO backbone

Why it ranks here: Cyware owns the sharing lane: the infrastructure behind many ISACs and ISAOs, bidirectional intel exchange with governance, and a TIP-plus-orchestration stack that moves verdicts to controls.

For sector collectives and enterprises running hub-and-spoke intel with subsidiaries, it’s the purpose-built answer.

Pros: Sharing infrastructure; ISAC pedigree; orchestration ties.

Cons: Solo-enterprise buyers use half the platform.

Bottom line: Collective defense, productized.

6. ThreatQuotient — Best Data-Driven Intel Library

Snapshot: Platform licensing | ThreatQ library + ACE scoring | Securonix-adjacent ownership note

Why it ranks here: ThreatQ built the intel library pattern: everything into one deduplicated, scored repository; adaptive scoring that learns from analyst decisions; and integrations marketplace pushing verdicts stack-wide.

Note the ownership landscape has shifted (Securonix acquisition) confirm roadmap continuity in procurement.

Pros: Library model clarity; adaptive scoring; integration marketplace.

Cons: Post-acquisition roadmap diligence required.

Bottom line: The classic TIP pattern, still clean verify the roadmap.

7. EclecticIQ — Best Analyst-Centric STIX-Native TIP

Snapshot: Platform licensing | STIX-native graph workbench | Gov/CERT pedigree

Why it ranks here: EclecticIQ serves the analyst who thinks in STIX: native structured-intel modeling, graph pivoting across entities, and the European government/CERT pedigree that shows in its rigor. It’s the craftsman’s TIP strongest where analysis quality, not feed volume, is the product.

Pros: STIX fidelity; analyst workbench; sovereign-sector fit.

Cons: Less turnkey for feed-consumer teams.

Bottom line: For intel teams that produce, not just consume.

8. Palo Alto (Cortex) — Best Suite-Embedded Intel Engine

Snapshot: Suite module | Unit 42 intel + TIM in Cortex | AutoFocus lineage

Why it ranks here: Palo Alto folds threat-intel management into Cortex: Unit 42’s research stream, TIM operationalizing indicators across XSOAR playbooks, and enforcement reach into the firewall estate no neutral TIP matches.

It’s intel as a suite layer compelling inside Palo Alto gravity, secondary outside it.

Pros: Enforcement reach; Unit 42 stream; XSOAR fusion.

Cons: Suite-coupled by design.

Bottom line: Intel that ends in a firewall rule.

9. Flashpoint — Best Deep/Dark-Web Intelligence

Snapshot: Subscription collections | Underground communities coverage | Fraud/physical convergence

Why it ranks here: Flashpoint’s collectors live where threats are planned: closed forums, markets, messaging channels.

The platform packages that access with analyst support for fraud, ransomware-extortion tracking, and physical-security convergence. As a primary TIP it’s narrower; as the underground lens in a stack, it’s the standard.

Pros: Underground access depth; fraud convergence; analyst services.

Cons: Complements rather than replaces a general TIP.

Bottom line: The dark-web telescope.

10. Intel 471 — Best Cybercrime-Underground Coverage

Snapshot: Intelligence subscriptions | Adversary/malware/credential intel | Actor-tracking methodology

Why it ranks here: Intel 471 tracks the cybercrime economy like a beat reporter: actor handles, malware-as-a-service supply chains, credential markets, and the HUMINT-grade sourcing that automated collectors miss.

Programs defending against monetized crime finance, retail, logistics get disproportionate value.

Pros: HUMINT depth; crime-economy mapping; credential-market visibility.

Cons: Specialist lens, not full-spectrum TIP.

Bottom line: Follow the money this is who’s watching it.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Score Relevance, Not Volume

Feed count is vanity; the metric that matters is what percentage of pushed indicators your estate could actually encounter.

Structure the program in two layers one neutral aggregation platform (Anomali, ThreatConnect, ThreatQuotient, EclecticIQ, Cyware) fusing everything, plus one or two primary-source providers (Recorded Future, Mandiant, Flashpoint, Intel 471) matched to your threat model and resist buying five overlapping feeds before measuring overlap.

In the pilot, demand a relevance test: have each platform score a month of its intel against your industry, stack, and geography, then count how many scored-critical items your SIEM could have matched.

Wire the TIP to push, not just store SIEM enrichment, SOAR verdicts, firewall and DNS blocklists and measure time-from-publication-to-control.

Confirm the ThreatQuotient ownership roadmap in writing, and remember the quiet ROI: deduplication alone often pays for the platform by cutting false-positive enrichment calls.

FAQs

What are the best threat intelligence platforms in 2026? Recorded Future leads on collection and graph depth; Anomali for retro-matching, ThreatConnect for intel-ops workflow, Mandiant for frontline sourcing, with Cyware, ThreatQuotient, EclecticIQ, Cortex, Flashpoint, and Intel 471 by lane.

TIP versus threat intel feed what’s the difference? Feeds are content; a TIP is the machinery that fuses, dedupes, scores, and pushes that content into controls and workflow.

How many intel sources do we need? One neutral aggregation layer plus one or two primary providers matched to your threat model measured overlap should stay under ~30% before adding more.

What’s the best TIP success metric? Time from intel publication to control update, and the percentage of pushed indicators relevant to your estate.

Do small teams need a TIP? Below a dedicated intel analyst, a TIP is usually premature suite-embedded intel (Cortex, Sentinel, SecOps) covers the basics until the function exists.

Verdict

Ten platforms, two layers, one discipline: intelligence only counts when it reaches a control before the attacker reaches you.

Recorded Future for breadth, Anomali for retro-truth, ThreatConnect for workflow, Mandiant for frontline authority, Cyware for sharing, ThreatQuotient and EclecticIQ for the library and the analyst, Cortex for enforcement, Flashpoint and Intel 471 for the underground fuse once, score against yourself, push everywhere, and measure the minutes.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
SOAR grew up twice: first from scripts to playbooks, then in the current wave from playbooks to AI agents that draft, decide, and act under human guardrails.

The 2026 field splits into suite engines living inside SIEM/XDR platforms and independent automation fabrics (Tines, Torq, Swimlane) selling speed-to-build to any stack. Palo Alto Cortex XSOAR takes 1 on depth and content gravity; Splunk SOAR and Tines complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Cortex XSOAR the deepest playbook ecosystem and marketplace in the category.

• Podium: XSOAR (depth), Splunk SOAR (SIEM-fused automation), Tines (fastest no-code build velocity).

• Market split: suite-embedded SOAR (Sentinel, Splunk, FortiSOAR) versus independent fabrics (Tines, Torq, Swimlane, D3) pick by stack gravity versus neutrality.

• 2026 theme: agentic AI automation platforms racing to let LLM agents execute tier-1 triage with auditable guardrails.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data. Criteria: playbook/automation depth, integration breadth, build velocity (time from idea to running workflow), AI-agent maturity, case management, and pricing accessibility.

Weights: automation depth 25%, build velocity 20%, integrations 20%, AI maturity 20%, case management 15%.

The 2026 SOAR Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Palo Alto Cortex XSOAR — Best Playbook Depth & Ecosystem

Snapshot: Platform licensing | Largest content marketplace | XSIAM convergence path

Why it earns 1: XSOAR remains the category’s reference: hundreds of content packs, a marketplace rivals haven’t matched,war-room case management, and playbook depth that handles the ugly edge cases simple workflows punt on.

Its gravity now pulls toward XSIAM, where SOAR becomes a layer of a converged SOC platform buyers should ask which SKU carries the roadmap.

Pros: Content ecosystem; playbook depth; case management maturity; threat-intel fusion.

Cons: Platform weight and cost for small teams; XSIAM-era packaging questions.

Bottom line: The most automation per playbook if you can feed the platform.

2. Splunk SOAR — Best SIEM-Fused Automation

Snapshot: Per-seat/event licensing | Native Splunk ES integration | Cisco portfolio ties

Why it ranks here: For Splunk estates the case is short: detections in ES trigger SOAR playbooks natively, context flows without connector glue, and the automation layer inherits Splunk’s content maturity.

Under Cisco the roadmap adds network-action reach. Outside Splunk estates, the independents win on neutrality and build speed.

Pros: SIEM fusion; mature playbook library; Cisco action surface.

Cons: Strongest only inside Splunk gravity.

Bottom line: The default when Splunk is the SOC’s spine.

3. Tines — Best No-Code Build Velocity

Snapshot: Story-based tiers, generous free tier | No-code canvas | AI workflow steps

Why it ranks here: Tines made automation a product anyone on the team can ship: seven building blocks, a canvas instead of code, and workflows live in an afternoon that playbook platforms would scope in weeks.

Its free tier seeded a practitioner community, and AI steps slot into stories under explicit control. Case management is deliberately lean pair with your ticketing spine.

Pros: Fastest idea-to-running-workflow; practitioner-loved; transparent tiers.

Cons: Lean case management; deep-custom logic eventually wants code.

Bottom line: The velocity pick — automation as a daily habit, not a project.

4. Torq — Best Agentic-AI Automation Fabric

Snapshot: Workflow/usage tiers | Hyperautomation + AI agents | Multi-agent orchestration

Why it ranks here: Torq leaned hardest into the agentic wave: socoteria-style AI runbooks where LLM agents triage, enrich, and close tier-1 cases under policy guardrails, with human escalation baked in.

The no-code fabric underneath matches the velocity leaders; the AI layer is the bet that differentiates it. Validate agent-autonomy claims against your own alert mix.

Pros: Agentic-AI depth; build speed; modern integration fabric.

Cons: Agent-autonomy claims need your-environment validation.

Bottom line: The AI-forward pick for teams ready to delegate tier-1.

5. Microsoft Sentinel — Best Bundled Estate Automation

Snapshot: Consumption (Logic Apps) | Sentinel-native playbooks | Copilot automation path

Why it ranks here: For Sentinel shops, SOAR arrives bundled: Logic Apps playbooks trigger from analytics rules, a connector catalog spanning the Azure estate, and Copilot threading AI assistance into response.

Costing is consumption-granular and the ceiling is real complex SOC workflow wants the dedicated platforms but the marginal price of starting is near zero.

Pros: Bundled economics; estate-native triggers; connector breadth.

Cons: Workflow depth and case management trail dedicated SOAR.

Bottom line: Start here if you’re already in Sentinel; graduate if workflows outgrow it.

6. Google SecOps SOAR — Best Case-Centric Suite SOAR

Snapshot: Suite packaging | Siemplify lineage | Gemini-assisted response

Why it ranks here: The Siemplify acquisition gave Google a genuinely case-centric SOAR: alert grouping into threat-centric cases, analyst workbench ergonomics, and now native fusion with SecOps SIEM and Mandiant intel.

Inside the Google SecOps suite it’s a clean story; as standalone SOAR, the independents iterate faster.

Pros: Case-grouping model; suite fusion; Gemini assistance.

Cons: Tied to suite gravity; standalone roadmap secondary.

Bottom line: The right SOAR if Google SecOps is your SIEM answer.

7. Swimlane — Best Low-Code at Enterprise Scale

Snapshot: Platform licensing | Turbine engine | Beyond-SOC automation reach

Why it ranks here: Swimlane’s Turbine pitches low-code automation at enterprise case volume high-throughput event processing, flexible data models, and use cases stretching past the SOC into fraud, compliance, and OT workflows.

It wins complex, high-scale automation programs; lighter teams find the platform more than they need.

Pros: Throughput scale; data-model flexibility; beyond-SOC reach.

Cons: Platform weight for small teams.

Bottom line: Enterprise automation programs, not quick wins.

8. Fortinet FortiSOAR — Best Fabric-Integrated SOAR

Snapshot: Appliance/VM/SaaS licensing ] | Security Fabric native | OT-aware playbooks

Why it ranks here: FortiSOAR completes the Fortinet story: playbooks that action FortiGate, FortiEDR, and the wider Fabric natively, with connector breadth beyond the family and OT-conscious content for the industrial estates Fortinet serves.

Outside Fortinet gravity it competes on price; inside, it’s the path of least resistance.

Pros: Fabric-native actions; OT content; value pricing.

Cons: Strongest case is Fortinet-estate-specific.

Bottom line: The Fabric estate’s automation layer.

9. Rapid7 InsightConnect — Best Mid-Market Bundled Automation

Snapshot: Per-user/workflow tiers | Insight platform native | Pre-built workflow library

Why it ranks here: InsightConnect extends Rapid7’s bundle logic to automation: pre-built workflows for the common 80%,native triggers from InsightIDR and InsightVM, and pricing a mid-market budget survives.

Depth-ceiling applies heavy custom orchestration belongs upstream but the time-to-first-automation is short.

Pros: Bundle economics; quick starts; platform-native triggers.

Cons: Custom-depth ceiling.

Bottom line: Automation for teams that already buy Rapid7.

10. D3 Security — Best MSSP-Grade Case Automation

Snapshot: Tiered platform licensing | Smart SOAR, multi-tenant | MITRE-mapped playbooks

Why it ranks here: D3 built for the service-provider pattern: multi-tenant case management, codeless playbooks mapped to ATT&CK, and event-pipeline automation that normalizes noisy client stacks.

MSSPs and large internal SOCs running many estates get leverage; single-tenant buyers have flashier options above.

Pros: Multi-tenancy; ATT&CK-mapped content; pipeline normalization.

Cons: Brand gravity trails the leaders.

Bottom line: The MSSP workhorse.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Automate the Boring 80% First

SOAR programs die from over-ambition: the six-month mega-playbook that never ships. Start with the five alerts that eat the most analyst-minutes per week phishing triage, IP enrichment, account-disable, EDR containment, ticket hygiene and demand each finalist demonstrate those five live, built in front of you, during the pilot.

That one request separates velocity platforms from services engagements. Decide the suite-versus-independent question by stack honesty: two-plus years committed to one SIEM favors its embedded SOAR; a mixed or shifting stack favors Tines/Torq-class neutrality.

For agentic AI, require audit trails and approval gates per action class before any autonomy, and measure the only number that matters: analyst-hours returned per week, published monthly.

FAQs

What are the best SOAR tools in 2026? Cortex XSOAR leads on depth, Splunk SOAR for SIEM fusion, Tines for build velocity, Torq for agentic AI, with Sentinel, Google SecOps SOAR, Swimlane, FortiSOAR, InsightConnect, and D3 by stack and scale.

Suite SOAR or independent? Committed single-SIEM estates lean suite (native triggers, bundled cost); mixed stacks lean independent fabrics for neutrality and speed.

Are AI agents ready for tier-1 triage? Ready for guardrailed delegation enrichment, grouping, draft verdicts with human sign-off on containment; full autonomy should be earned per playbook with audit trails.

What should a SOAR pilot prove? Your five noisiest workflows, built live during the pilot, with time-to-build and analyst-hours-saved measured.

Does SOAR replace analysts? No it converts their hours from copy-paste to judgment; the headcount story is capacity reclaimed, not seats cut.

Verdict

Ten platforms, two buying lanes, one metric: analyst-hours returned. XSOAR for maximum depth, Splunk and Sentinel and Google for suite gravity, Tines and Torq for the speed-and-AI frontier, Swimlane for enterprise scale, FortiSOAR for Fabric estates, InsightConnect for the mid-market, D3 for MSSPs ship the boring 80% first, gate the AI with audit trails, and publish the hours you got back.
