articles.description:
Hackers have abused government and school domains to promote illegal gambling websites, creating unauthorized subdomains while leaving the institutions’ main websites running normally. Two unrelated operations used changes to Domain Name System (DNS) records to place gambling pages beneath trusted institutional addresses, borrowing their reputation to attract visitors through search results. The activity affected institutions […]

The post Hackers Hijack Government and School Subdomains to Promote Illegal Gambling Websites appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers have abused government and school domains to promote illegal gambling websites, creating unauthorized subdomains while leaving the institutions’ main websites running normally.

Two unrelated operations used changes to Domain Name System (DNS) records to place gambling pages beneath trusted institutional addresses, borrowing their reputation to attract visitors through search results.

The activity affected institutions in Bangladesh, India, and Mexico. One operation involved more than 850 observed entry points across eight institutional domains and connections to over 30 gambling brands.

These figures describe infrastructure, not confirmed victims or infections, and researchers consider them minimum counts because their investigation was continuing.

Researchers from Infoblox identified the two operations and detailed their findings in an October 26, 2026, report on domain shadowing.

The research describes DNS abuse supporting illegal gambling promotion, rather than a newly identified malware family. How the attackers initially gained access to DNS administration remains unknown.

Hackers Hijack Government and School Subdomains

Domain shadowing allows attackers to add unauthorized DNS records beneath a legitimate domain without changing its main website.

Unlike the previously reported Hazy Hawk subdomain hijacking activity involving abandoned cloud resources, these operations appear to involve unauthorized access to DNS administration. That distinction matters when investigating how control was obtained.

Infoblox tracks the first actor as Hidden Hawk, which appears to sell search visibility to illegal Indonesian gambling brands.

The actor added CNAME records, which make one hostname an alias for another, beneath school and government domains. Most pointed to gambling content hosted externally on Cloudflare Pages rather than institutional servers.

The external hosting names often copied the corresponding institutional hostname, replacing dots with hyphens. This pattern helped researchers reconstruct relationships between the hijacked addresses and hosted pages.

In one documented example, gambling content remained accessible beneath a Bangladeshi secondary school’s domain between July 6 and October 1, 2026.

The use of legitimate hosting services also appears in separate Cloudflare Pages scam campaigns that exploit readily available infrastructure. Here, the important feature was the connection between externally hosted gambling pages and trusted institutional addresses.

Website checks alone could miss the activity because the schools’ and government offices’ primary services remained available. Six Bangladeshi school domains carried approximately 50 to more than 240 entries each, while a Mexican educational domain had over 50.

A Kerala government subdomain hosted gambling content directly and received some school CNAME connections. Researchers observed the Kerala case as remediated in July 2026, although some other infrastructure remained active.

During controlled research, Infoblox contacted a Telegram account believed to belong to Hidden Hawk using a fabricated casino identity.

The operator offered backlink optimization, custom landing pages, and Google AMP pages, supplied payment details, and guaranteed a top Google ranking. Researchers made no payment; the sales pitch matched the infrastructure they observed.

Government DNS Delegations Expanded Attacker Control

The second operation targeted Maharashtra government infrastructure and an ESIC subdomain in India. Rather than adding individual aliases, the attackers created unauthorized nameserver delegations to ClouDNS.

This transferred authority over selected DNS subzones to external nameservers, allowing records beneath them to be managed outside the government’s normal DNS environment. Infoblox has not attributed this activity to Hidden Hawk.

A wildcard record expanded that control by allowing arbitrary names beneath one delegated subzone to resolve.

Gambling-related records appeared from at least August 2025. Content delivery involved DigitalOcean, Amazon CloudFront, and BunnyCDN, with machine-generated doorway pages covering rummy, betting, lotteries, and satta matka.

The delegations disappeared by mid-October 2026, suggesting remediation. The findings add to concerns about gambling infrastructure, although separate casino sites concealing espionage demonstrate a different use of similar-looking content.

In this investigation, the documented purpose was search visibility and traffic acquisition. The evidence does not establish that visitors received malware, or that either operation stole institutional data.

For defenders, the priority is monitoring authoritative DNS changes, not simply checking whether a homepage looks normal.

Unexpected CNAME targets, new nameserver delegations, unexplained wildcard records, and bursts of unfamiliar subdomains require investigation. Certificate-transparency observations should also be compared with approved services and DNS change records.

Organizations discovering unauthorized changes should remove the offending records, review registrar and DNS-provider logs, rotate exposed credentials, and enforce multifactor authentication.

Infoblox cautions against blocking entire legitimate institutional domains. Response should focus on unauthorized hostnames and attacker-controlled infrastructure while addressing the account access or delegation that enabled the abuse. Shared hosting platforms likewise require contextual investigation rather than blanket blocking.

The post Top 10 Best Ransomware Recovery Solutions in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Prevention lost; now what? That question not backup-window math defines ransomware recovery, a discipline measured in hours-to-business and judged on three hard problems: finding the clean restore point, proving it’s actually clean, and rebuilding at scale without reinfecting yourself.

We scored ten platforms specifically on the recovery day, not the backup night. Rubrik takes 1; Veeam and HPE Zerto complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Rubrik clean-point identification and blast-radius analytics built for the worst day.

• Podium: Rubrik (recovery intelligence), Veeam (verified restores at breadth), Zerto (near-zero RPO rewind).

• Different metric than backup: this list ranks hours-to-business after an attack, not protection breadth see our Backup & Recovery ranking for that lens.

• Reinfection is the silent second incident: clean-room staging and snapshot scanning separate real recovery platforms from restore buttons.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation: clean-point identification (anomaly/encryption analytics on snapshots), restore verification and clean-room staging, recovery speed at scale (mass-restore orchestration, failover), blast-radius and sensitive-data assessment, and pricing structure.

No lab testing; no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Weights: clean-point intelligence 30%, recovery speed 25%, verification/clean-room 20%, orchestration maturity 15%, pricing clarity 10%.

The 2026 Ransomware Recovery Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Rubrik — Best Recovery Intelligence

Snapshot: Subscription | Anomaly detection, blast-radius, sensitive-data exposure | Default-immutable

Why it earns 1: Recovery day is an intelligence problem before it’s a restore problem, and Rubrik answers the three questions that matter fastest: when did encryption start (anomaly timeline), what did the attacker touch (blast radius), and what data was exposed (sensitive-data discovery on snapshots).

clean-point selection backed by that evidence turns a guessing game into a procedure.

Pros: Best-in-class clean-point analytics; immutability by default; quarantine-aware restores.

Cons: Premium pricing; full value on its platform model.

Bottom line: The worst-day decision-support leader.

2. Veeam — Best Verified Restore at Breadth

Snapshot: Subscription | SureBackup verification, malware scanning, orchestrated DR | Broadest estate reach

Why it earns 2: Veeam proves restores before the crisis automated recovery verification, malware scanning on backup data, and orchestrated recovery plans across more workload types than anyone.

When the estate is heterogeneous, Veeam is usually the platform that can actually rebuild all of it.

Pros: Verification discipline; orchestration (Recovery Orchestrator); estate breadth.

Cons: Deepest analytics arrived later than Rubrik’s.

Bottom line: Rehearsed recovery across everything you run.

3. HPE (Zerto) — Best Near-Zero RPO Rewind

Snapshot: Quote/subscription | Continuous data protection | Journal-based any-second rewind

Why it earns 3: Zerto’s continuous journal lets you rewind to seconds before encryption began an RPO class snapshots can’t touch.

For revenue-critical applications where losing four hours of transactions is its own disaster, journal-based recovery is the difference-maker, now under HPE’s umbrella.

Pros: Seconds-level RPO; fast failover orchestration; encryption-detection triggers.

Cons: Journal economics scope it to tier-1 apps.

Bottom line: Rewind the tape to the second before impact.

4. Cohesity — Best Snapshot Threat Analytics

Snapshot: Quote | Threat scanning + classification on backup data | Veritas-merged vendor

Why it earns 4: Cohesity turned the backup corpus into a hunting ground threat scanning + classification on backup data, IOC scanning, ML anomaly detection, and classification over snapshots so clean-point selection is evidence-driven. Post-Veritas-merger scale broadens reach; roadmap diligence applies.

Pros: Strong threat analytics on snapshots; cyber-vault options.

Cons: Post-merger portfolio clarity.

Bottom line: Hunt the attacker inside your backups.

5. Commvault — Best Cleanroom Recovery

Snapshot: Subscription | Cleanroom recovery environments | Threat scanning + deception sensors

Why it earns 5: Commvault operationalized the step most programs improvise: an isolated cleanroom where restores are staged, scanned, and validated before touching production paired with early-warning deception and threat scanning across its broad workload matrix.

Pros: Cleanroom as product, not project; coverage depth.

Cons: Platform complexity reputation.

Bottom line: Rebuild in quarantine, then promote with confidence.

6. Druva — Best SaaS-Isolated Recovery

Snapshot: Per-workload SaaS | Backup estate outside your blast radius | Curated snapshots + quarantine

Why it earns 6: Druva’s recovery advantage is architectural: the backup platform lives in its cloud, not your compromised network, so the attacker who owns your domain can’t reach it.

Curated clean snapshots, quarantine, and accelerated-response tooling ride on that isolation.

Pros: Blast-radius isolation by design; zero recovery infrastructure to rebuild.

Cons: Massive on-prem restores bound by bandwidth planning.

Bottom line: Recovery capacity the attacker never touched.

7. Dell — Best Vault-Based Recovery

Snapshot: Quote | PowerProtect Cyber Recovery vault + CyberSense analytics

Why it earns 7: Dell’s vault pattern air-gapped copies analyzed by PowerProtect Cyber Recovery vault + CyberSense analytics gives boards and regulators a recovery story they can diagram: a sealed room of known-good data, scanned for corruption, ready for staged rebuild.

Pros: Mature air-gap architecture; integrity analytics; auditor-legible design.

Cons: Infrastructure-heavy; vault sizing discipline required.

Bottom line: The sealed-vault recovery pattern, productized.

8. IBM FlashSystem — Best Array-Speed Restores

Snapshot: Array-based | Safeguarded Copy immutable snapshots | Fast storage-level recovery

Why it earns 8: When ransomware strikes and terabytes of data need restoring, IBM FlashSystem helps businesses recover quickly using Safeguarded Copy.

Its protected snapshots cannot be modified or deleted through normal host access, even if production systems are compromised.

Storage-level recovery reduces dependence on slower traditional backup restores, making it a strong recovery layer for critical enterprise workloads.

Pros: Protected immutable snapshots; fast storage-level recovery; strong ransomware resilience.

Cons: Requires compatible IBM FlashSystem infrastructure; not a complete ransomware recovery platform.

Bottom line: Fast, protected recovery built directly into enterprise storage.

9. Acronis — Best SMB Recovery Blend

Snapshot: Published tiers | One-click recovery + active anti-ransomware | MSP-aligned

Why it earns 9: For SMBs and MSPs, Acronis compresses the whole cycle one-click recovery + active anti-ransomware that halts encryption, then one-click full-image recovery into one agent at published prices, which is the right shape when there’s no recovery team, just a Tuesday.

Pros: Integrated prevent+recover; accessible pricing; MSP tooling.

Cons: Enterprise orchestration depth limited.

Bottom line: The small-team recovery answer that actually gets deployed.

10. Index Engines — Best Independent Integrity Verification

Snapshot: Quote/OEM | CyberSense analytics | Validates backups across vendors

Why it earns 10: Index Engines plays referee: its CyberSense engine (also OEM’d in Dell’s vault) inspects backup content for corruption patterns with high published accuracy claims, independently of whichever backup vendor made the copies the second opinion a recovery decision deserves.

Pros: Vendor-independent integrity verdicts; deep content inspection.

Cons: Analytics layer, not a restore engine.

Bottom line: Proof your “clean” point is actually clean.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Script the Worst Tuesday, Then Time It

Buy for the sequence, not the features: detection flags encryption → analytics identify the last clean point → integrity verification proves it → restores stage in isolation → validated workloads promote to production.

Walk every finalist through that exact sequence on your estate and demand timings.

Tier your applications first journal-based CDP (Zerto-class) for the revenue tier, snapshot platforms for the bulk, array-speed layers (Pure-class) where volume dominates.

Insist on immutability that survives stolen admin credentials, and add independent verification (Index Engines-class) if a wrong clean-point call would be existential. Then rehearse twice a year with the real on-call roster; the plan that lives in a PDF recovers nothing.

FAQs

What is the best ransomware recovery solution in 2026? Rubrik ranks 1 for clean-point intelligence, Veeam for verified restores across the broadest estates, and HPE Zerto for seconds-level rewind on tier-1 applications with Commvault’s cleanroom and Dell’s vault leading their patterns.

How is this different from the best backup solution? Backup rankings weigh protection breadth and operations; recovery rankings weigh the attack day clean-point identification, verification, and hours-to-business. Strong vendors appear on both lists for different reasons.

What’s a clean restore point and why is it hard? The last snapshot before attacker activity hard because dwell time means the attacker predates the encryption event, so you need analytics on backup history, not just timestamps.

How do you avoid restoring the infection? Stage restores in an isolated clean room, scan with independent analytics, rotate credentials before promotion, and never restore identity systems first without forensic validation.

What RPO should we target? Tier it: seconds (CDP) for revenue-critical transactions, hours (snapshots) for the bulk estate. Uniform RPO targets overspend on the many and underprotect the few.

Verdict

Rubrik tells you where clean lives, Veeam proves restores before you bet on them, Zerto rewinds the seconds that matter, and Index Engines referees everyone’s claims rank your finalists by stopwatch on your own worst-Tuesday script, because recovery is the one control whose demo is the incident.

Ransomware crews attack backups before they attack production encrypting or deleting recovery points first, then ransoming what’s left.

That inverted kill chain has turned backup from an infrastructure checkbox into a security control, judged now by immutability, blast-radius isolation, and verified restore speed rather than backup-window math.

Our source sheet listed ten vendors, but Cohesity’s merger with Veritas makes them one company so this is an honest Top 9, with Veeam at 1 and Rubrik and the combined Cohesity-Veritas completing the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Veeam the ubiquity leader, with immutability and recovery verification across the broadest estate mix.

• Podium: Veeam (breadth), Rubrik (security-first architecture), Cohesity Veritas (combined-scale data protection).

• Consolidation alert: Cohesity + Veritas merged into one data-protection giant we rank them as one vendor, not two.

• The test that matters: a timed, clean-room restore of a real workload not a dashboard of green checkmarks.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation: immutability and isolation options, ransomware detection/response integration, restore speed and verification, workload coverage (VM, SaaS, cloud, physical), operational simplicity, and pricing structure. No lab testing; no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Weights: cyber-resilience features 30%, restore confidence 25%, workload coverage 20%, operational simplicity 15%, pricing clarity 10%.

The 2026 Backup & Recovery Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Veeam — Best Overall Breadth + Resilience

Snapshot: Licensed/subscription | VMs, physical, cloud, M365, Kubernetes (Kasten) | Hardened repositories

Why it earns 1: Veeam protects more estate shapes than anyone vSphere to Azure to Microsoft 365 to Kubernetes and has pushed hard into cyber-resilience: immutable hardened repositories, malware detection on backup streams, and SureBackup-style recovery verification that proves restores before you need them.

Ubiquity also means hiring, community, and runbook depth no rival matches.

Pros: Broadest workload coverage; strong immutability story; proven restore verification; huge ecosystem.

Cons: Portfolio sprawl can complicate licensing choices.

Bottom line: The default that keeps re-earning its spot.

2. Rubrik — Best Security-First Backup

Snapshot: Subscription | Zero-trust architecture | Anomaly detection + sensitive-data visibility

Why it earns 2: Rubrik built for the inverted kill chain: backups immutable by architectural default (not an option to configure), ransomware anomaly detection on every snapshot, blast-radius assessment, and quarantine-aware recovery.

It markets as a cyber-resilience company rather than a backup vendor, and the product substance largely matches the framing.

Pros: Immutability by default; strong attack-detection analytics; clean operational model.

Cons: Premium positioning; deepest value on its appliance/cloud model.

Bottom line: Backup designed assuming the attacker is already inside.

3. Cohesity Veritas — Best Combined-Scale Platform

Snapshot: Quote | Cohesity’s modern platform + Veritas NetBackup’s enterprise base | One vendor post-merger

Why it earns 3: Our sheet listed Cohesity and Veritas separately, but the completed merger makes them one data-protection giant NetBackup’s vast enterprise and heterogeneous-workload footprint joined to Cohesity’s hyperconverged, security-analytics-rich platform.

The combination is formidable; the integration roadmap (which console, which repository format, migration paths for NetBackup estates) is the diligence item every buyer should put in writing.

Pros: Enormous combined coverage; Cohesity’s threat-analytics layer; NetBackup’s legacy reach.

Cons: Post-merger roadmap and portfolio-rationalization uncertainty.

Bottom line: One vendor now make the integration roadmap contractual.

4. Commvault — Best Enterprise Coverage Depth

Snapshot: Subscription/quote | Broadest workload matrix | Cleanroom recovery + threat scanning

Why it earns 4: Commvault’s workload matrix databases, SaaS, hypervisors, mainframe-adjacent, every major cloud remains among the deepest in the industry, and its cyber-resilience additions (cleanroom recovery environments, threat scanning,cloud-native SaaS delivery via its platform evolution) keep the veteran current.

Pros: Coverage depth few match; cleanroom recovery concept; mature enterprise operations.

Cons: Complexity reputation persists despite simplification work.

Bottom line: When the estate is genuinely heterogeneous, Commvault usually covers all of it.

5. Druva — Best SaaS-Delivered Backup

Snapshot: Per-workload subscription | 100% SaaS | No backup infrastructure to own

Why it earns 5: Druva deleted the backup infrastructure problem: endpoints, M365, AWS workloads, and data-center sources protected into its cloud with zero appliances to patch which also means the backup estate can’t be encrypted by the attacker who owns your network, a quietly powerful ransomware property.

Pros: No infrastructure to attack or maintain; clean per-workload economics; fast deployment.

Cons: Very large on-prem estates may outgrow the model.

Bottom line: Backup as a utility, isolated from your blast radius by design.

6. Dell (PowerProtect) — Best Vaulted Infrastructure

Snapshot: Quote | Data Domain dedupe heritage + Cyber Recovery vault

Why it earns 6: Dell’s answer is physics: PowerProtect appliances with industry-reference deduplication, and the Cyber Recovery vault an air-gapped, analytics-scanned copy environment that regulators and boards understand instantly.

For Dell-standardized data centers, it’s the straightforward hardened path.

Pros: Proven vault architecture; dedupe economics at scale; Dell ecosystem integration.

Cons: Infrastructure-heavy model in a SaaS-shifting market.

Bottom line: The air-gap answer you can point an auditor at.

7. Acronis — Best Backup + Endpoint Security Blend

Snapshot: Published tiers | Backup fused with anti-malware + patching | Strong MSP channel

Why it earns 7: Acronis merges backup with active anti-ransomware protection, patching, and endpoint hygiene in one agent a cyber-protection blend that fits SMBs and the MSPs who serve them, at published prices the enterprise anchors won’t print.

Pros: Integrated protection + recovery; MSP-friendly; transparent pricing.

Cons: Enterprise data-center depth below the anchors.

Bottom line: The SMB/MSP lane’s two-jobs-one-agent answer.

8. Microsoft — Best Azure/M365-Native Floor

Snapshot: Consumption-based | Azure Backup + M365 native capabilities

Why it earns 8: Azure Backup covers Azure VMs, SQL, and files with vault immutability, and Microsoft 365 ships retention primitives a genuine floor for Microsoft-centric estates.

But native M365 retention is not full backup (no true point-in-time restore guarantees across all services), which is exactly why the vendors above sell M365 backup. Know where the floor ends.

Pros: Native integration; consumption pricing; vault immutability.

Cons: M365 “backup” gaps; Azure-scoped reach.

Bottom line: Use the floor; don’t mistake it for the building.

9. NetApp — Best Array-Integrated Protection

Snapshot: Licensed with arrays | SnapMirror/SnapVault + autonomous ransomware protection

Why it earns 9: On NetApp estates, protection lives in the storage layer: near-instant snapshots, replication, and on-array autonomous ransomware detection that flags encryption behavior as it happens. It’s the deepest answer for ONTAP shops and, honestly, scoped to them.

Pros: Snapshot speed and efficiency; on-array ransomware detection; mature replication.

Cons: Value concentrated in NetApp-standardized estates.

Bottom line: If you run ONTAP, start here; if not, look above.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Time a Restore Before You Trust a Dashboard

Green backup dashboards survive every breach; restores are what fail. Before signing, run a timed, clean-room recovery of one production-class workload database plus application tier and measure hours-to-usable, because that number is your real ransomware exposure.

Demand immutability that an attacker with admin credentials cannot disable (architectural, like Rubrik’s, or hardened/vaulted, like Veeam’s and Dell’s not a checkbox a stolen account can untick).

Cover Microsoft 365 explicitly; native retention is a floor with documented gaps. If you’re a NetBackup or Cohesity customer, get the merged company’s integration roadmap in writing at renewal.

And rehearse the full ransomware day detection on backup streams, scope assessment, clean-point identification, staged restore twice a year, with the people who’d actually do it.

FAQs

What is the best backup and recovery solution in 2026? Veeam ranks 1 for breadth plus cyber-resilience depth, Rubrik for security-first architecture, and the merged Cohesity Veritas for combined enterprise scale with Druva leading the SaaS-delivered lane and Acronis the SMB/MSP blend.

Why do we rank 9 vendors, not 10? Our source list named Cohesity and Veritas separately, but their completed merger makes them one vendor. We consolidated the entry rather than inflate the count.

What makes backup “ransomware-proof”? Immutability an admin credential can’t disable, isolation from the production blast radius, detection on backup streams, and verified restores. Any one alone is marketing; the four together are resilience.

Is Microsoft 365’s built-in retention enough? No it’s retention, not full point-in-time backup across all services. Every vendor on this list sells M365 backup because the native floor has documented gaps.

How often should restores be tested? Quarterly timed tests of representative workloads, plus a twice-yearly full ransomware-day rehearsal including clean-point identification. Untested backups are hypotheses.

Verdict

Veeam covers everything and verifies it, Rubrik assumes the attacker is inside and builds accordingly, and Cohesity Veritas is now one giant whose roadmap belongs in your contract whichever you pick, buy immutability credentials can’t untick, and judge the product by a stopwatch on a restore, not a dashboard of green.

articles.title: Sony Suffers Massive Data Breach – 2.58 Million So-net and Plala Users’ Data Exposed
articles.description:
Sony Network Communications has confirmed a breach exposing 2,585,481 customer records linked to its So-net and plala (S Course) internet services. The company disclosed the incident on October 27, 2026, after finding unauthorized access to its member database. The exposed information includes contact details, account identifiers, and passwords for selected email services. According to the […]

The post Sony Suffers Massive Data Breach – 2.58 Million So-net and Plala Users’ Data Exposed appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Sony Network Communications has confirmed a breach exposing 2,585,481 customer records linked to its So-net and plala (S Course) internet services.

The company disclosed the incident on October 27, 2026, after finding unauthorized access to its member database. The exposed information includes contact details, account identifiers, and passwords for selected email services.

According to the official So-net notice, the breach affected 2,141,986 So-net records and 443,495 plala records. These figures reflect customer records, not a verified count of unique individuals. Former subscribers are also affected, widening the impact beyond people still using the services.

The leaked member information includes names, telephone numbers, email addresses, user IDs, dates of birth, gender, and internet connection IDs.

Sony said the breach did not expose passwords associated with the main membership accounts. The compromised data did not include credit card information.

Sony Suffers Massive Data Breach

According to reports, credentials for 54,401 email accounts across four Sony services were exposed: Mail Service (G) (24,655), A-Box (17,672), So-net VAIO Mail (7,005), and PostPet Mail (5,069). Sony reset the affected passwords on October 27 to prevent misuse.

CNET Japan reported that the exposed email credentials could have allowed someone to read, send, and receive messages through email software or So-net Webmail.

This does not establish that attackers actually accessed those mailboxes. Users must set new passwords and update saved credentials in their email applications.

Sony also confirmed exposure of 16 bank account records containing details such as bank names, branch information, account numbers, and account holder names.

Bank PINs were not stored. Seven records involving password reset notification documents were also exposed, prompting password resets for those affected.

The unauthorized access occurred on October 19. Sony identified the intrusion on October 23, stopped the affected servers, and blocked communications from the source. Investigators confirmed the information leak and established the affected data categories and counts on October 24.

Sony reported the incident to Japan’s Personal Information Protection Commission. The company has not disclosed how the attacker entered, a specific software flaw, or the attacker’s identity.

Its investigation into the cause and full impact remains ongoing. No information leak involving NURO or other services outside the named groups has been confirmed.

The incident is separate from the previously reported Sony MOVEit data breach, which involved Sony Interactive Entertainment and a different system. No connection between the incidents has been established.

The affected records include 272,215 former So-net members and 21,130 former plala members who canceled from March 2026 onward. Sony said customers who canceled by February 2026 were not affected.

Exposed personal details can fuel convincing scams, so phishing prevention is important. Customers should open the official account website directly, reset passwords for affected email accounts, and avoid unexpected links or attachments. As of October 27, Sony confirmed no resulting secondary harm but warned that suspicious messages could follow.

articles.title: Hackers Target U.S. Election Commission, Forcing Online System Shutdown Days Before Midterms
articles.description:
Hackers targeting the U.S. Federal Election Commission forced officials to shut down its electronic filing system days before the November 3 midterm elections, blocking campaign finance disclosures during a critical spending period. The disruption affects how political committees report money flowing into races, not how Americans vote. The FEC does not run elections, and Reuters […]

The post Hackers Target U.S. Election Commission, Forcing Online System Shutdown Days Before Midterms  appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers targeting the U.S. Federal Election Commission forced officials to shut down its electronic filing system days before the November 3 midterm elections, blocking campaign finance disclosures during a critical spending period.

The disruption affects how political committees report money flowing into races, not how Americans vote. The FEC does not run elections, and Reuters says the outage should not affect voters’ ability to cast ballots, according to Reuters.

The shutdown began late on October 26 after campaign compliance staff could no longer submit mandatory reports. An email Reuters reviewed described an active attempt to break into agency systems. “We have a bad actor attempting to breach FEC systems. As a result, we’ve had to temporarily shut down our web-facing services,” an FEC electronic filings officer told several compliance firms.

Hackers Target U.S. Election Commission

The FEC’s official status page recorded an investigation into the electronic filing outage at 10:15 p.m. Eastern time on October 26. Further updates followed overnight and the next morning. At 8:17 p.m. Eastern on October 27, officials said they had identified the issue and were implementing a fix. However, that message did not confirm a completed recovery, and the incident remained listed as unresolved.

The agency said its IT staff were working to restore service, while previously filed reports remained available for public searches. That distinction matters. The confirmed disruption affects submitting new disclosures, not access to existing campaign finance records. The status page also listed a related FECfile+ submission outage, showing that officials were tracking problems affecting filing services.

Public details remain limited. Neither the FEC statement nor the reporting reviewed identifies the attackers, their location, their entry method, or a specific software flaw.

Those sources also provide no public confirmation that attackers stole records, changed filings, deployed ransomware, or gained lasting access. The email describes an attempted breach and a defensive shutdown, which should not be mistaken for proof of a successful data breach.

Technically, the key distinction is between an attacker directly disabling a service and defenders taking it offline to contain a suspected threat. The available account supports the latter. It does not establish whether malicious traffic, stolen credentials, or an application flaw triggered the response. Assigning a particular attack method before investigators release evidence would go beyond the facts currently available.

Earlier incidents show why clear distinctions matter. Cybersecurity News previously covered the UK Electoral Commission breach, where attackers accessed email systems and electoral register copies. That case involved confirmed access to stored information. No comparable disclosure has been made for this FEC incident, and no evidence links the two cases.

The immediate cost is reduced transparency. The outage prevents organizations from submitting 24-hour and 48-hour spending reports, which help reveal who is paying to influence individual races. Steven Mele, president and CEO of compliance firm MBA Consulting Group, told Reuters he had never seen anything like it in 26 years.

The timing makes the disruption especially serious. OpenSecrets research director Brendan Glavin told Reuters that super PACs and dark money groups spent more than $50 million on average per day over the previous week. On October 20 alone, more than $250 million was reported. Delayed filings leave voters and watchdogs with less timely information about that spending.

Political cyber incidents can have different goals. Previous reporting on the Trump campaign hack described an attributed Iranian operation. No such attribution exists here. For now, the central questions are when filing access will return and what investigators can establish about the attempted intrusion. Clear recovery updates will help separate verified findings from speculation as Election Day approaches.

articles.description:
Hackers have quietly planted malware in 42 real GitHub repositories. The traps fire when a developer opens a project with Claude, Gemini, Cursor, or VS Code. The repositories belong to 11 legitimate owners, including individual developers, students, and one company. The hidden code sits in a file named .github/init.js, and it is huge, between 12.9 […]

The post Hackers Hijack 42 GitHub Repositories to Plant Malware Traps for Claude, Gemini, and Cursor Users appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers have quietly planted malware in 42 real GitHub repositories. The traps fire when a developer opens a project with Claude, Gemini, Cursor, or VS Code. The repositories belong to 11 legitimate owners, including individual developers, students, and one company.

The hidden code sits in a file named .github/init.js, and it is huge, between 12.9 MB and 13.7 MB. Small settings files for each tool call this script when a session starts or a folder opens.

Developers already worry about GitHub comment prompt injection that tricks AI agents, but this case needs no clever prompt. It simply abuses the startup hooks that the tools trust.

Researchers at JFrog Security Research identified the armed repositories while digging into an npm worm they track as the “testmetest” campaign.

Another firm, SafeDep, had first described the npm side on October 22 and reported no confirmed victims. JFrog’s look at the GitHub side showed that real repositories had already been armed.

Hackers Hijack 42 GitHub Repositories

The payload is a rebuild of a hidden CI publisher called ci.js. A CI publisher is a script that runs inside GitHub Actions and pushes new packages to npm.

JFrog says the operator wanted to turn stolen GitHub and npm access into fresh malicious releases, which then feed more stolen access back into the loop. The same TrapDoor supply chain campaign also aimed at AI coding assistants, so this trick is not entirely new.

In each victim repository, the hook files wait for a trigger. The Claude settings file, for example, runs node .github/init.js || bun .github/init.js at session start.

Matching triggers were placed for Gemini, Cursor’s MCP configuration, and VS Code folder-open tasks. Some projects also had package.json, composer.json, or Makefile changes. In plain terms, a normal habit like opening a workspace could run the payload.

The files stayed hidden because of their size. GitHub code search did not index the huge blobs, and the contents API could not return them.

JFrog’s first sweep found 26 repositories, and the files looked empty. Checking the repository trees directly raised the total to 42. The Register also covered the findings.

All 10 wrapper variants decode to the same payload, so the size differences do not change what it does. The attacker also faked history. On September 28, scripted batches copied old commit messages and dates from real history and added skip-checks:true. That made the activity look much older than it was.

Stolen Accounts, Native Addons and cPanel Links

JFrog traced several hijacked identities. One account, leamasuero, belonged to a developer with real work history from 2014 to 2022.

By July 2026 it was used for testing, and on September 28 the attacker renamed repositories and armed 13 of them in two minutes. In the company account, Crayon-Biz-LLP, commits came from at least two members, which suggests several stolen credentials.

The npm side also changed tactics. Three packages carry a compiled native addon and an encrypted file called .napi_cache. The addon decrypts it with the XOR key 0x96, drops a script into a temporary folder, and runs it in the background.

It stays asleep on CI systems, containers, small virtual machines, and debuggers, so automated scanners miss it. The Windows build also checks for tools such as Wireshark, Fiddler, and x64dbg. This is the kind of trusted-looking bait seen in the fake AI tool campaign that targets developers.

JFrog also found scanner workflows in the same hijacked accounts. They download a tool to /tmp/.svc and scan for cPanel and WHM systems vulnerable to CVE-2026-41940, an authentication bypass.

JFrog found no proof that any cPanel server was actually breached. The link is operational, and not one proven chain from every npm infection to the exploit.

Defenders should remove the malicious package versions and rebuild affected systems from trusted sources. They should rotate GitHub, npm, cloud, SSH, and AI-provider credentials, and check every reachable repository for the hook files above.

Teams should read repository trees directly instead of relying on search. They should also watch for HalluSquatting poisoning AI assistants, since AI tools can be steered toward fake resources.

One order matters: remove the net-health-checker and pkg-runtime persistence before revoking the stolen GitHub token, because the worm contains a token-revocation wiper.

New York, NY, October 27th, 2026, CyberNewswire

The root-cause fix will take weeks; protection can’t wait

Sweet Security today announced Sweet Safety Net, extending its runtime Virtual Patching protection to every organization affected by HTTP2Shell (CVE-2026-111497).

The capability will enable users to block any exploitation of Node2Shell at no cost for 30 days, whether or not they are Sweet customers. 

HTTP2Shell sits inside the Brotli decoder built into Node.js, Bun, Python, Envoy, Istio and, as Sweet’s own research revealed this week, Go frameworks such as Traefik, Fiber and Iris.

Patching it everywhere will take weeks. Sweet Safety Net gives affected teams protection at the vulnerable code path, with no code changes, no commitment, while engineering ships the permanent fix.

Sweet Security is already observing active exploitation attempts across 88% of monitored environments. 

“We are watching HTTP2Shell exploitation attempts in real environments right now,” said Dror Kashti, CEO and co-founder of Sweet Security.

“We’re extending our protection to organizations that need help securing affected applications. Sweet Safety Net exists because every organization deserves the same visibility and protection our customers have – especially in a moment like this. Virtual Patching closes the exploitation path today. The permanent fix can follow.”

The Root-Cause Fix Will Take Weeks. Protection Can’t Wait.

HTTP2Shell lives in the Brotli decoder compiled into the runtimes and libraries that applications are built on.

Fixing it at the root means updating every affected dependency, rebuilding applications that bundle the decoder, testing the changes and redeploying them across production.

For most organizations, that will take weeks. For the whole time, the vulnerable code keeps running and stays reachable by attackers.

Sweet’s Virtual Patching closes that gap with a surgical fix at runtime. Instead of waiting for the code to change, Sweet stops the attack payload before it reaches the vulnerable code path, and legitimate traffic keeps flowing.

The bug is still in the code, but it can no longer be exploited. 

Teams get protection now and can ship the permanent fix on their own timeline, without the pressure of an open exposure. 

What Virtual Patching Does

Sweet Security’s Virtual Patching protects running applications while engineering completes the permanent fix.

Sweet applies a protection policy through its sensor, targeting the vulnerable code path and blocking exploitation while legitimate traffic continues. No application code change is required.

Teams apply the policy from Sweet’s Vulnerabilities Catalog, and Sweet distributes it to sensors on each node running the affected workload.

Once the sensors confirm enforcement, the workload is marked Protected from that vulnerability. Protection follows the workload as it scales and restarts.

Sweet customers can use the Vulnerabilities Catalog to apply protection to affected workloads and confirm enforcement through the Protected status.

Sweet Security customers are already protected. Sweet’s runtime sensors and L7 detection rules are active across all customer tenants, with exploitation attempts already detected and blocked in monitored environments.

The Sweet Safety Net

Effective immediately, any organization can claim Sweet Security sensors with Virtual Patching protection for 30 days. No purchase commitment is required.

To claim the offer, please visit: https://hi.sweet.security/http2shell-virtual-patching-sweet-safety-net#activate 

About Sweet Security

Sweet Security delivers a proactive runtime security platform for cloud and AI. By understanding how applications, identities, and AI agents behave in live environments, Sweet helps security teams discover what’s running, prove which weaknesses attackers can exploit before it happens, harden their defenses, and stop malicious activity in real time.

Trusted by the world’s leading AI companies to secure the next frontier, Sweet gives organizations the visibility and control to adopt new technologies with confidence while protecting the systems their businesses depend on.

The warning followed a breach involving malicious programs on customer servers and an extortion demand of approximately ¥8 billion. The attackers threatened to publish customer information […]

The post Japan’s GMO Internet Urges Customers to Shut Down PCs After Hackers Threaten Ransomware Attack appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Japan’s GMO Internet urged customers of its Onamae.com Desktop Cloud service to disconnect their PCs, shut them down, and unplug connected cables after suspected attackers threatened a ransomware attack.

The warning followed a breach involving malicious programs on customer servers and an extortion demand of approximately ¥8 billion.

The attackers threatened to publish customer information and launch ransomware at noon Japan Standard Time on October 27, 2026.

GMO later confirmed that alleged company and customer information appeared online at 12:30 p.m. However, its update at 1:55 p.m. said no ransomware attack had been confirmed, and the published material was still being checked.

GMO Internet Group researchers noted that they were examining customer devices for malware, including ransomware.

Importantly, the company’s ninth incident response report said no malware had been found on devices whose analysis was complete by 11:59 a.m. That finding did not establish that every customer’s computer was safe.

Japan’s GMO Internet Urges Customers

GMO’s shutdown request was a precaution against a threatened attack, not confirmation that ransomware had spread across customers’ personal computers.

The distinction matters: malicious programs had been confirmed in some hosted server environments, while investigators were separately checking customer devices.

The company asked users to scan their systems, back up data, disconnect network connections, and switch off their PCs. The disruption follows other Japanese incidents where companies stopped services to limit damage.

During the Niconico cyberattack service suspension, operator Dwango also took its platform offline while investigating. Such shutdowns interrupt normal activity, but GMO’s warning focused on reducing customers’ exposure while the scope of the compromise remained uncertain.

According to GMO’s initial unauthorized access notice, the company confirmed malicious programs in some customer server environments on October 20.

It identified 26,739 servers as potentially affected and began shutting down servers across all Desktop Cloud plans from 4 a.m. on October 21. Information stored inside those environments could have been viewed.

That server count should not be read as a confirmed number of infected personal computers or customers whose data was stolen.

GMO’s first notice described potential server exposure, while later updates addressed device investigations and alleged leaked information. The company has not publicly connected those categories through a verified, final victim count in the notices reviewed.

GMO received the threatening email demanding approximately ¥8 billion on October 21 and consulted police the following day.

It refused payment, explaining that meeting the attackers’ demands would not guarantee deletion of stolen information or prevent misuse. The company continued coordinating with investigators and relevant authorities as its response expanded.

Device Investigation, Account Protection, and Recovery

GMO employees collected customer devices across Japan after requesting cooperation on October 25. Its white-hat hacker team began examining the submitted systems, with more devices expected.

Trend Micro and AI companies offered assistance, although GMO described the details of their involvement as still being coordinated rather than announcing a completed joint investigation.

Backups formed another part of GMO’s customer guidance. Separate reporting on ransomware operators disabling backups explains why recovery systems deserve protection alongside endpoints.

That broader behavior has not been attributed to the GMO attackers; the company’s public notices did not identify a ransomware family, a backup-destruction technique, or an encryption mechanism.

Customers were also told to change credentials stored or used on affected servers, including passwords reused elsewhere. GMO warned that it would never request passwords or authentication codes and urged users to distrust messages offering paid recovery.

Its tenth report advised checking official notices instead of opening links or files in incident-related emails or text messages.

Recovery commitments included a previously announced ¥5,000 payment and replacement PCs of equivalent performance for customers whose ransomware damage was verified.

These measures do not prove ransomware occurred. Meanwhile, Google’s air-gapped backup vaults illustrate how separating protected recovery copies from ordinary workloads can support resilience, although GMO did not announce use of that technology.
